entries.meaning: One part in three of something, and the model for every fraction used the same way.
examples: A third of the seats were still empty when the lights went down.
Two-thirds of the roof came off in the first hour of the storm.
She paid a third at signing and the balance on delivery.
Of the forty applications, roughly a third were incomplete.
Three-quarters of them had never heard of the company before that week.
He read a quarter of it, decided it was hopeless, and gave the book away.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and never stressed, and before of the phrase runs together — a third of it /əˈθɚdəvɪt/, uh-THUR-duh-vit. The compound fractions keep two beats and a hyphen in print: two-thirds /ˌtu ˈθɚdz/, too-THURDZ; three-quarters /ˌθri ˈkwɔrtɚz/, three-KWOR-turz
entries.русский: треть — одна часть из трёх; так же устроены все дроби: a quarter «четверть»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: fractional quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a third of the budget, an ordinary count noun, cut it into thirds, and, in the third to arrive, the ordinal)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass or a sum
entries.refers to: one part in three of a set or a quantity — the members of a set of countables (plural) or an amount of a mass (singular). Every other fraction works the same way: a quarter, two-thirds, three-quarters, a fifth, seven-eighths.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — A third of the seats were empty (countable → plural); A third of the budget is gone (mass → singular). The numerator does not decide it either: Two-thirds of the members have signed is plural because members is, and Two-thirds of the roof was torn off is singular because roof is. The of-phrase decides, exactly as with half, all, and most.
entries.pattern: a third [verb] · a third of [determiner + noun] · a third of [object pronoun] · [verb] a third · about a third, nearly two-thirds, a good third, the bottom third · by a third, by two-thirds (adverbial)
entries.variants: a quarter and a fourth (both standard American, a quarter the commoner outside arithmetic class), two-thirds, three-quarters, a fifth, three-eighths, and every other fraction built on the same frame
entries.contrast: Against half: half is the one fraction that may drop the of in front of a determiner — half the time is standard and ✗a third the time is not, so the phrase has to be a third of the time. Against some and most: those are vague on purpose, while a fraction reads as a claim about proportion and a reader will treat it as one — write about a third when the number is an estimate. On the page a two-word fraction standing alone takes a hyphen (two-thirds of them, three-quarters were sold), while a third and a quarter need none. And keep the fraction apart from the ordinal: the third of the applicants is a portion, the third applicant is a position in line.
entries.see also: half, all, most, some, the rest, the majority, the whole, a quarter, a third, two-thirds (determiner), half (determiner)

entries.meaning: Names the complete quantity or the complete membership of something, leaving nothing out.
examples: All of the tickets were sold before noon.
Of the forty crates we shipped, all arrived intact.
She read the file and sent copies to all of us before the meeting.
She spent all of it on rent.
All of the paint had dried in the can.
That's all I have to say about it.
All I want is a straight answer.
All are welcome at the Sunday service.

senses.head: The entire number of a set of countables
examples: All of the tickets were sold before noon.
Of the forty crates we shipped, all arrived intact.
She read the file and sent copies to all of us before the meeting.

senses.head: The entire amount of a mass or abstraction
examples: She spent all of it on rent.
All of the paint had dried in the can.

senses.head: Everything, with a relative clause
body: The verb stays singular even when the complement after it is plural — All I want is answers — because the subject is the whole clause all I want. The plural by attraction, All I want are answers, is common and turns up in edited prose; the singular is the safer choice and the one an editor will leave alone.
examples: That's all I have to say about it.
All I want is a straight answer.

senses.head: Everybody — formal and ceremonial only
examples: All are welcome at the Sunday service.

entries.pronunciation note: no reduced vowel of its own, but it runs into what follows: all of them /ˈɔl əvəm/ · AW-luh-vum
entries.русский: всё; все — вся совокупность счётного множества или вся масса целиком
entries.case: none — one invariable form for subject and object
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, all children, and a predeterminer, all the children)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant in form; construes as plural with countables and singular with a mass or an abstraction
entries.refers to: the entirety of a set of countable things or people (plural), the whole of a mass or abstract quantity (singular), or everything covered by a following relative clause (all that remains, all I know). Bare all meaning "everybody" survives only in formal or ceremonial writing — All are welcome.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to. Countable referent → plural verb: All of the seats are taken. Mass or abstract referent → singular verb: All of the money is gone; All I need is a break. The of-phrase decides, not the word all.
entries.pattern: all [verb] · all of [determiner + noun] · all of [object pronoun] · [verb] all · all [relative clause] (all that remains) · that's all · floated after the subject: they all left, we have all seen it
entries.contrast: Against each and every one: all takes the members together and goes plural (All of them are here), while each and every one take them one at a time and go singular (Each of them is here) — same fact, different packaging. Against half and none: the three mark the whole of an of-phrase, half of it, and none of it, and all three take their number from it. Against whole: all of the cake is every piece of it; the whole cake is the cake as an undivided thing. Where the of is required and where it is not: before a pronoun it is obligatory — all of them, ✗all them — but before a determiner all is a predeterminer and may drop it, so all the seats and all of the seats are equally standard, exactly as with both and half. In we all left and he thanked us all, all has floated out of the noun phrase and needs no of either. The dialect all them apples is a different thing again — the object pronoun them doing a determiner's job, systematic in Southern and Appalachian vernacular and in African American English, and nonstandard in every register of writing.
entries.see also: both, half, none, each, every one, most, some, everything, all (determiner)

entries.meaning: Everybody in sight, named as a crowd rather than as people.
examples: He announced the engagement to all and sundry before telling his mother.
All and sundry were welcome at the open house, which turned out to be the problem.
She has explained the plan to all and sundry, and nobody is any the wiser.
The gate was left open and all and sundry wandered in off the street.
Terms of the settlement were emailed to all and sundry by mistake.
It stops being a secret the moment you tell all and sundry.
entries.pronunciation note: the and is always reduced to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n̩/ and is never said in full; the main beat falls on sundry
entries.русский: все кому не лень, все без разбора — книжн.-шутл., преим. брит.; только о людях
entries.register: formal-jocular, and chiefly British; an American meets it in British writing, in legal boilerplate, and in deliberately arch journalism
entries.type: fixed quantifying pronoun phrase meaning "everyone, without distinction" (the adjective sundry survives almost nowhere else outside the determiner of sundry expenses)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: every person in sight, taken as an undifferentiated crowd — invited or not. People only: ✗all and sundry of the boxes.
entries.agreement: plural, always — All and sundry were invited; All and sundry have had their say. ✗All and sundry is is wrong even though the phrase names a lump.
entries.pattern: all and sundry [plural verb] · [verb] all and sundry (He told all and sundry) · to all and sundry · no of-phrase at all: ✗all and sundry of them
entries.contrast: Against one and all: the same crowd with the opposite attitude — one and all welcomes them, all and sundry complains about them. Against plain everyone: that is the neutral word, singular in agreement, and the one to use unless the archness is wanted. The legal doublet all and singular is a third relative and is pure boilerplate. Note that the phrase takes no of: for a specific set the pronoun is all of them.
entries.see also: one and all, all, every one, everyone, everybody, all and singular (determiner), sundry (determiner)

entries.meaning: Every item in the list just given.
examples: Payment may be made by cash, check, credit card, or all of the above.
All of the above are covered under the standard warranty.
Was it the wiring, the roof, or the foundation? — All of the above.
If all of the above is correct, mark option (d).
She was asked whether she was tired, hungry, or annoyed, and answered all of the above.
Bring your license, your registration, and proof of insurance; all of the above must be current.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /əv/ and then to /ə/, and the before the vowel of above is /ði/
entries.русский: всё вышеперечисленное — отсылка к списку выше, язык анкет и тестов
entries.register: neutral; the native language of forms, tests, and slides, and a stock joke in speech
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase, deictic — it points at a list on the page rather than at anything in the world
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with the listed items and singular when the list is treated as one answer
entries.refers to: everything in a list just given — the lines above it on a page, a form, or a screen. Its antecedent is textual, which is why the phrase is nearly useless in conversation and indispensable on paper.
entries.agreement: plural with the items, singular with the option — All of the above are covered by the warranty (the things listed); All of the above is correct (the whole list as a single choice). Both are standard, and the plural is the safer default whenever the list is a list of things.
entries.pattern: all of the above [verb] · [verb] all of the above · standing alone as a multiple-choice option ((d) all of the above) · the parallel forms none of the above, any of the above, some of the above, both of the above
entries.contrast: Against none of the above and any of the above: one list, and the three phrases answer how much of it exactly as all, none, and any do for a set of things. The above is functioning as a noun here, so the article cannot be dropped: ✗all of above. And because the antecedent is on the page, a reader who has scrolled past the list has lost it — in running prose, name the items instead.
entries.see also: none of the above, any of the above, all, every one, none, all of (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points at two things at once and insists on the fact that there are two — plain the two reports the pair, both emphasizes that neither one is left out.
examples: Both were accepted, which nobody had expected.
I've read both of them twice.
She offered me coffee and tea, and I took both.
The lawyers agreed, but both wanted it in writing.
Both of my sisters live in Chicago now.
She sent the signed contract to both of them by noon.
Paperback or hardcover? — Both, if that's an option.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; before a consonant the final /θ/ often drops in casual speech — both times /boʊ ˈtaɪmz/
entries.русский: оба, обе — ровно двое уже названных; не о массе и не о трёх и более
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, both books, a predeterminer, both the books, and half of the correlative both … and)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; always plural — it refers to exactly two
entries.refers to: exactly two countable things or people, already identified. Never a mass (✗both of the water) and never three or more (✗both of the triplets — use all three).
entries.agreement: plural, always — Both are ready; Both of the applications were rejected. There is no context in which ✗both is is correct.
entries.pattern: both [plural verb] · both of [determiner + plural noun] · both of [object pronoun] · [verb] both · floated after the subject: they both agreed, they have both agreed, he told us both
entries.the negation trap: Both of them didn't pass is genuinely ambiguous — it can mean neither passed or only one did. Write Neither of them passed or Only one of them passed and the ambiguity disappears. Before a pronoun, of is required when both heads the phrase (both of them, ✗both them); them both and they both are the floated forms and are equally standard.
entries.contrast: Both = the two together (plural verb); each = the two taken one at a time (singular verb); either = one or the other; neither = not one and not the other.
entries.see also: all, half, each, either, neither, each other, both (determiner)

entries.meaning: Absolutely everybody, named as a crowd nobody invited.
examples: Everyone and their mother was at the lake that weekend.
By Tuesday everyone and their mother had an opinion about the new logo.
She posted it once and everyone and their brother shared it.
I wanted a quiet table, and what we got was everyone and their mother.
Everyone and their mother has a podcast now.
He told everyone and their mother before he told his own department.
entries.pronunciation note: the and is always reduced to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n̩/ and is never said in full, their weakens to /ðɚ/ in fast speech, and the main beat falls on mother
entries.русский: все кому не лень, полгорода — разг.-шутл., о нелепо большой толпе людей
entries.register: informal and jocular — speech, social media, and casual writing, almost always with a complaint or a joke attached; never in edited prose, where the word is everyone
entries.type: hyperbolic quantifying pronoun phrase meaning "absolutely everybody"
entries.person / number: third person; singular in agreement in ordinary use, because the phrase is felt as one emphatic everyone
entries.refers to: every person imaginable, presented as an absurdly large crowd. People only — there is no ✗everything and its mother.
entries.agreement: singular is the ordinary choice — Everyone and their mother was at the lake; Everyone and their mother has a podcast now. The plural (were, have) also occurs and is what an ordinary and-coordination would predict; since the phrase is barred from formal writing anyway, no editor is going to arbitrate between them. The their inside the phrase is singular they pointing back at everyone, which is standard American English.
entries.pattern: everyone and their mother [verb] · [verb] everyone and their mother · everyone and their mother's + noun (everyone and their mother's opinion) · no of-phrase at all: ✗everyone and their mother of them
entries.variants: everybody and their mother, everyone and their brother, everybody and his brother (the older form, and one that generic he has been retreating from for forty years), everyone and their dog, everyone and their uncle; British and Australian English says every man and his dog
entries.contrast: Against all and sundry: the same crowd in a formal-jocular register instead of a casual American one, and both of them faintly disgusted. Against one and all: warm and ceremonial where this is exasperated. Against plain everyone: the neutral word, singular in agreement, and the one to write when nothing is being exaggerated. Note that the exaggeration is the entire content of the phrase — it adds no members to everyone, which already has all of them, and that logical impossibility is exactly the joke.
entries.see also: all and sundry, one and all, all, every one, every last one, everyone, everybody, they (generic)

entries.meaning: One of the two equal parts of something — or, in loose everyday use, roughly that much.
examples: Half of the seats were still empty at kickoff.
She read half of it on the plane and finished the rest at home.
Half of the cake was gone before the candles came out.
Of the forty applications, half were incomplete.
He split the fee with her and kept half for himself.
She had already sent a copy to half of them before anyone objected.
entries.pronunciation note: the l is silent. The broad vowel /hɑf/ · HAHF survives in Eastern New England and is the ordinary British form; the noun's plural is halves /hævz/. Before of the phrase runs together: half of them /ˈhæfəvəm/ · HAF-uh-vum
entries.русский: половина — одна из двух равных частей; в речи и просто «добрая половина»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: fractional quantifying pronoun (also a determiner and a predeterminer, half the time, a count noun, two halves, and an adverb, half finished)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: one of the two equal parts of a set or a quantity — countable things or people (plural), or a mass (singular). In ordinary speech it also does duty for "roughly half" and even "a large part" (Half of them never showed up), which is idiomatic English and not an arithmetic claim.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — Half of the seats were empty (countable → plural); Half of the cake was gone (mass → singular). Bare Half is enough is singular on a mass reading and Half are missing plural on a count reading. The of-phrase decides, exactly as with all, some, and most.
entries.pattern: half [verb] · half of [determiner + noun] · half of [object pronoun] · half [determiner + noun] with no of (predeterminer: half the time, half my life) · [verb] half · half and half · in half, by half, the better half
entries.contrast: Half is one of the three words in this dictionary — with all and both — that can drop the of in front of a determiner: half the time and half of the time are both standard, and the shorter one is the more idiomatic in speech. Before a pronoun the of comes straight back and is obligatory: half of them, ✗half them. Against all and none: the three of them mark the whole of a set, half of it, and none of it, and all three take their number from the referent. Keep the pronoun apart from the count noun half, which has a real plural (cut it into halves, the first half). And note that half an hour and a half hour are both standard American English, while ✗a half an hour is a blend of the two that editors delete on sight.
entries.see also: all, both, none, most, some, less, half (determiner)

entries.meaning: Not a single one — the old rural negative, still alive in Southern and Appalachian speech.
examples: We hunted morels all afternoon and found nary a one.
He asked six neighbors for help, and nary a one would come.
Of all the promises made that spring, nary a one was kept.
There were supposed to be eggs in the coop; there was nary a one.
Nary a one of them had ever set foot in the county.
She counted the tools twice, and nary a one was missing.
entries.pronunciation note: nary is a worn-down ne'er a, "never a," so the article is already inside the word and the second a is always the reduced /ə/
entries.русский: ни один, ни единого — диал. и устар., южноамериканская сельская речь
entries.register: regional and dated — Southern, Appalachian, and older rural American speech; in print it appears as dialect writing, as quoted speech, or as a deliberate folksy flourish, and it is not standard edited English
entries.type: negative quantifying pronoun phrase
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: not a single member of a set of countable things or people. Never a mass: ✗nary a one of the water.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Nary a one was left; Nary a one of them has called.
entries.pattern: nary a one [singular verb] · nary a one of [determiner + plural noun] · nary a one of [object pronoun] · [verb] nary a one · the determiner nary a + singular noun (nary a soul, nary a dime), which is where most readers meet the word at all
entries.variants: ary a one (its positive twin, since ary means "any" — Have you got ary a one?); nary one and the eye-dialect narra one
entries.contrast: Against not a one: the same phrase in national colloquial American English, with no regional marking on it. Against none and not one: those are the neutral words, usable in every register. Where an American meets it. In the South and in Appalachia it is ordinary speech, commoner from older speakers than from younger ones; everywhere else it survives in fiction, in country lyrics, and in journalism quoting either. Inside those varieties it carries no stigma at all; outside them it reads as a costume, so in edited prose the word is none.
entries.see also: not a one, not one, none, no one, nothing, nary a (determiner), ary / ary a (determiner)

entries.meaning: Says that not one member of a set qualifies, or that not any of a quantity is left.
examples: None of the applicants had the certification.
None of the milk was left by Sunday.
I looked for a charger, but there was none in the drawer.
None of the three explanations is convincing.
Of the forty seats, none were empty.
She read all three offers and accepted none of them.
She asked for volunteers, and none came forward.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; a homophone of nun
entries.русский: ни один; нисколько — ничто из множества или массы под отрицанием
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: negative quantifying pronoun — and pronoun only: unlike all, some, and most, it has no determiner use at all, because in front of a noun the word is no (no money, ✗none money)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural — see below
entries.refers to: the members of a set of countables (people or things) or the amount of a mass, inside the scope of negation. It handles both, which is what separates it from no one and nobody.
entries.agreement: either, and this is not a mistake. With a plural countable referent, both None of them is and None of them are are standard, and the plural is the more common choice in American usage — plural none has been in continuous use since Old English and is not a modern slackening. Use the singular when the sense you want is emphatically "not a single one" (None of the three candidates is acceptable), and the plural as the ordinary default (None of the windows were locked). With a mass referent it is singular only: None of the water was drinkable. The rule that none must always be singular because it comes from not one is a zombie rule — it was invented in the eighteenth century and never described real usage. A conservative editor may still prefer the singular in formal writing; neither form will be marked wrong.
entries.pattern: none of [determiner + noun] · none of [object pronoun] · none [verb] (None survived) · [verb] none · none but [noun phrase] (formal) · none other than [name] · none the wiser, none too pleased (adverbial idioms, a different word class)
entries.contrast: Against no one and nobody: those two refer to people only and are always singular; none covers things and mass quantities as well and takes either number. Against neither: use neither when the set has exactly two (Neither of the twins was hurt), none for three or more. Against no: no is the determiner (no money), none the pronoun (I have none) — the two are in complementary distribution, so ✗I have no and ✗none money are both impossible.
entries.see also: all, half, any, neither, some, no one, nobody, nothing, no (determiner)

entries.meaning: Not one of the items in the list just given.
examples: (e) None of the above.
Which of these describes your symptoms? — None of the above.
None of the above applies to part-time employees.
He read the four explanations the report offered and believed none of the above.
Given the three finalists, most of the committee would have voted for none of the above.
If none of the above is correct, write your own answer on the line.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /əv/ or /ə/, and the before the vowel of above is /ði/
entries.русский: ничего из вышеперечисленного — последний вариант в тестах и бюллетенях
entries.register: neutral — the last option on a multiple-choice question, a line on some ballots, and a refusal in speech
entries.type: negative quantifying pronoun phrase, deictic
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural, exactly as none does
entries.refers to: not one of the items in a list just given. The antecedent is textual — lines on a page rather than things in the world.
entries.agreement: either. None of the above applies to me and None of the above apply to me are both standard, the same split that runs through none: the singular is the emphatic "not a single one," the plural the ordinary default.
entries.pattern: standing alone as an option ((e) none of the above) · none of the above [verb] · [verb] none of the above · on a ballot, a vote for none of the above
entries.contrast: Against all of the above and any of the above: one list, three quantities. Against bare none: none takes a set of things in the world, none of the above a set of lines on a page. Nevada prints a literal None of These Candidates line on its statewide ballots, which is where most Americans have seen the phrase used as a real choice rather than as a test answer; in ordinary speech it is a joke or a refusal, not a quantity.
entries.see also: all of the above, any of the above, none, not one, no one, nothing, none of (determiner)

entries.meaning: Not a single one, said with feeling.
examples: I asked around for a spare key and got not a one.
Not a one of those windows will open.
Sixty people were invited and not a one wrote back.
He has plenty of opinions and not a one worth hearing.
How many of the seedlings came up? — Not a one.
She went through the whole drawer, and there was not a one left.
entries.pronunciation note: the article reduces to /ə/, and in ordinary speech the /t/ of not is a flap or a glottal stop, nah-duh-WUN
entries.русский: ни один, ни единого — разг. амер.; в строгой прозе лучше not one или none
entries.register: colloquial American — unremarkable in speech and in quoted speech, a shade too casual for formal prose, where not one or none does the same work
entries.type: emphatic negative quantifying pronoun phrase
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: not a single member of a set of countable things or people. Never a mass: ✗not a one of the water.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Not a one was broken; Not a one of them has answered. The plural noun inside the of-phrase never pulls the verb over.
entries.pattern: not a one [singular verb] · not a one of [determiner + plural noun] · not a one of [object pronoun] · [verb] not a one · as a bare answer (How many came? — Not a one.)
entries.contrast: Against not one: the same meaning with the article added for emphasis, and that article is exactly what drops the register — Not one of them called is edited English, Not a one of them called is speech. Against none: the neutral, register-free word, and the only one of the four that also takes a mass. Against nary a one: that is the Southern and Appalachian version; not a one is the form used nationally.
entries.see also: not one, nary a one, none, no one, nothing, not a (determiner)

entries.meaning: Not a single one, with the count made an issue.
examples: Not one of the smoke detectors had a battery in it.
Twelve letters went out and not one came back.
Not one of us knew what the meeting was for.
She checked every seal, and not one had been broken.
He made four promises that spring and kept not one.
Not one of the three explanations survives a second reading.
entries.pronunciation note: both words carry stress, the heavier beat on one; the /t/ is commonly a glottal stop, nah(t)-WUN
entries.русский: ни один — эмфатический вариант none, уместен в любом стиле
entries.register: neutral — usable in every register, and the standard way to make none emphatic
entries.type: emphatic negative quantifying pronoun phrase — the negation of the pronoun one (also a determiner, not one drop)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: not a single member of a set of countable things or people. Never a mass: ✗not one of the sand.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Not one was returned; Not one of the machines is working. The plural noun inside the of-phrase cannot pull the verb over, and ✗Not one of the machines are working — common in speech — is the error to watch for.
entries.pattern: not one [singular verb] · not one of [determiner + plural noun] · not one of [object pronoun] · [verb] not one · fronted with inversion for emphasis (Not one of them did he trust) · not one but two, which corrects a count rather than denying it
entries.contrast: Against none: identical in meaning and different in force — None of the applicants were qualified reports the fact, Not one of the applicants was qualified insists on it, and that insistence is why the singular verb is obligatory here while none takes either number. Against not a one: the same emphasis one register lower. Against no one: that is people-only and does not take an of-phrase in current English — ✗no one of them; the form is not one of them.
entries.see also: not a one, nary a one, none, none of the above, every one, one, no one, not one (determiner)

entries.meaning: Everybody, greeted as a group and as individuals at once.
examples: Happy New Year to one and all.
One and all were invited to the reopening.
The mayor thanked one and all for turning out in the rain.
They stood and applauded, one and all.
Welcome, one and all, to the fortieth season.
The verdict pleased one and all except the defendant.
entries.pronunciation note: the and reduces to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n̩/; the main beat falls on all
entries.русский: все до одного, все и каждый — торжеств.-шутл., в тостах и приветствиях
entries.register: ceremonial and often jocular — toasts, welcomes, announcements, greeting cards; not ordinary conversational English
entries.type: fixed quantifying pronoun phrase meaning "everyone"
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: every person present or addressed, taken individually (one) and collectively (all) at the same time — the doubling is the whole point of the idiom. People only.
entries.agreement: plural — One and all are invited; One and all were on their feet. Standing in apposition to a subject, it takes that subject's number: They rose, one and all.
entries.pattern: one and all [plural verb] · [verb] one and all (Welcome, one and all) · in apposition after the subject (The staff, one and all, signed the card) · to one and all · as a vocative (Good evening, one and all) · no of-phrase: ✗one and all of them
entries.contrast: Against all and sundry: the same crowd from the other side — one and all is warm, all and sundry faintly disgusted. Against everyone: the neutral word, and singular in agreement (Everyone is invited), where this phrase is marked and plural (One and all are invited). Against each and every one: that is an emphatic distributive, singular, and it takes of (each and every one of them), where one and all takes none.
entries.see also: all and sundry, all, every one, each, everyone, everybody

entries.meaning: A thing taken entire, set against the parts it is made of. ---
examples: The whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
The whole of the estate went to a cousin nobody had met.
She spent the whole of the morning on hold with the county.
Two of the chapters are strong, but the whole never quite holds together.
The whole of the argument rests on a single mistranslated footnote.
He took the machine apart and could not put the whole back together.
On the whole, the repairs went better than anyone expected. (fixed adverbial, not the pronoun)
entries.pronunciation note: the w of whole is silent, so the takes its ordinary weak form /ðə/ before the consonant; the whole of it runs together as /ðə ˈhoʊləvɪt/, thuh HOH-luh-vit
entries.русский: целое, всё целиком — книжн., в противопоставлении частям; о людях не говорят
entries.register: formal to neutral; the bare pronoun belongs to writing about parts and wholes, and the everyday phrase for the same thing is all of it
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the adjective whole used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, the whole of the morning, an adjective, the whole loaf, and a count noun, a whole made of parts)
entries.person / number: third person; singular, always — it names one undivided thing, however many parts that thing has
entries.refers to: a thing taken entire and undivided, as against its parts — an object, a body of work, an estate, a stretch of time, an argument. Never a set of countables taken severally: ✗The whole of the guests were late; for that the word is all.
entries.agreement: singular, always — The whole is greater than the sum of its parts; The whole of the argument rests on one footnote. The verb stays singular even with a plural noun after of, as long as the sense is genuinely "the thing entire": The whole of the proceedings was recorded. Where a plural verb is what you want, the pronoun you want is all.
entries.pattern: the whole [singular verb] · the whole of [determiner + noun] · the whole of [object pronoun] · [verb] the whole · as a whole, on the whole, taken as a whole (fixed adverbials, not this pronoun) · the whole nine yards, the whole shebang (idioms built on the adjective)
entries.contrast: Against all: all takes the members of a set together and goes plural (All of the guests were late), while the whole takes one thing entire and stays singular — all of the cake is every piece of it, the whole cake is the cake as an undivided thing, which is the distinction the all entry points at from the other side. Against the rest and the remainder: those name what is left over, this names what was never divided. Against half and a third: the same axis with nothing cut off. And two frames are not this pronoun at all — on the whole and as a whole are fixed adverbials, and the whole day and the whole truth are the ordinary adjective in front of a noun.
entries.see also: all, half, a third, the rest, the remainder, the residue, none, everything, the whole (of) (determiner), whole (determiner)

entries.meaning: Picks the members of a known group out one at a time, so that whatever is said applies to every member separately.
examples: Each of the samples was tested twice.
She handed out the folders, and each contained a different contract.
Each of us has a copy of the key.
They each brought something to the potluck.
She handed a numbered folder to each of us as we came in.
Each was asked to sign before leaving the building.
The tickets are forty dollars each. (adverb of distribution, not the pronoun)
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form
entries.русский: каждый в отдельности — о членах определённого множества от двух и более
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: distributive pronoun (also a determiner, each student, a floating quantifier, they each got one, and an adverb of distribution, they cost five dollars each)
entries.person / number: third person; grammatically singular, always, however many members the set has
entries.refers to: the individual members of a definite set of two or more, considered separately — people or things, countables only. Never a mass: ✗each of the sand.
entries.one systematic exception: when each has floated out of the subject and sits after it, the subject is the plural pronoun and the verb is plural — They each have a key. For the pronoun referring back, singular they is standard American English: Each of them submitted their own draft.
entries.agreement: singular verb, always — Each is inspected before shipping; Each of the rooms has its own thermostat, never ✗have. The head of the phrase is each, not the plural noun inside the of-phrase.
entries.pattern: each of [determiner + plural noun] + singular verb · each of [object pronoun] · each [singular verb] · [plural subject] each [plural verb] (floated) · [plural subject] [auxiliary] each [verb] · [verb] [object] each (adverbial: cost a dollar each) · each other is a separate reciprocal pronoun
entries.contrast: Each vs. every — and why every is not in this dictionary. Every is a determiner only; it has no pronoun use whatsoever, so ✗Every was checked is ungrammatical and you must write Every one was checked in two words. Each is both determiner and pronoun. In meaning, each looks at the members one by one while every sweeps the whole set, which is why every accepts almost and nearly (almost every one) and each does not (✗almost each). Each also works for a set of exactly two (a ring on each hand), where every is odd. Each vs. both: Each of them is (singular) and Both of them are (plural) report the same fact with different grammar.
entries.see also: every one, either, neither, both, all, one, each other, each (determiner), every (determiner)

entries.meaning: Names one of two possibilities without saying which, usually because either one would do.
examples: Either of those dates works for me.
I asked both lawyers, and either would take the case.
Is either of them still open on Sundays?
You can take the bus or the train — either gets you there by six.
He didn't like either of the proposals.
If either of you hears from her, call me right away.
entries.pronunciation note: /i/ is the dominant American vowel and /aɪ/ a recognized variant, neither one wrong
entries.русский: любой из двух — один из ровно двух, безразлично какой
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: distributive pronoun (also a determiner, either side, half of the correlative either … or, and an adverb of negative agreement, I don't either)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: one of exactly two, with no commitment as to which — people or things, countables only. With three or more it is wrong: ✗either of the three; use any.
entries.agreement: singular in careful use — Either of the routes is fine; Is either of them available? Plural verbs after either of are common in speech and turn up in print, but a conservative editor will change them, so the singular is the safe choice everywhere. (Separately: when the correlative either … or joins two subjects, the verb agrees with the nearer one — Either the manager or the assistants are handling it. That is the conjunction, not this pronoun.)
entries.pattern: either of [determiner + plural noun] + singular verb · either of [object pronoun] · either [singular verb] · [verb] either · in questions: Is either of them …? · under negation: I don't want either
entries.contrast: Either = one of the two, choice open; neither = not one and not the other; both = the two together, plural verb. Under negation not … either is equivalent to neither: I don't want either = I want neither. Do not stretch it past two — with three or more the word is any. The either of a fence on either side means "each of two" and is the determiner, not this entry; the either of I don't like it either is an adverb.
entries.see also: neither, each, both, any, none, either (determiner)

entries.meaning: Every single member of a group, with the completeness made an issue.
examples: Every last one of the smoke detectors was dead.
She read the complaints, every last one, before she answered any of them.
They promised forty chairs and delivered every last one of them broken.
Every last one of us had been told a different story.
How many of the seedlings came up? — Every last one.
He kept the receipts for eleven years, every single one of them filed by month.
entries.pronunciation note: three beats with the main stress on one; the /t/ of last is regularly lost in the cluster in front of it, ev-ree-lass-WUN
entries.русский: все до единого — разг., подчёркивает отсутствие исключений; и о вещах тоже
entries.register: informal to neutral — ordinary in speech and in journalism, a shade too emphatic for a report
entries.type: emphatic quantifying pronoun phrase — the two-word every one with an intensifier wedged into it
entries.person / number: third person; singular, always
entries.refers to: every member of a definite set, with the absence of exceptions made the point — things as well as people, countables only. Never a mass: ✗every last one of the water.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Every last one was accounted for; Every last one of the bulbs has to be replaced. The plural noun inside the of-phrase never pulls the verb over, exactly as under every one. Referring back, singular they is standard: Every last one of the drivers renewed their license.
entries.pattern: every last one [singular verb] · every last one of [determiner + plural noun] · every last one of [object pronoun] · [verb] every last one (She read every last one) · as a bare answer (How many were broken? — Every last one.)
entries.variants: every single one (the commonest of the family and the most neutral of them), each and every one (the most formulaic, and the one editors cut), every blessed one and every damn one (stronger, and marked accordingly), and the fuller every last one of them
entries.contrast: Against plain every one: identical in meaning and different in force — Every one of them was returned reports the fact, Every last one of them was returned insists on it, usually with exasperation or triumph attached. Against all: all takes the set together and goes plural (All of them were returned), this takes it one member at a time and stays singular. Against not one and not a one: the same emphatic gesture on the other side of the negative. And note where the intensifier can go: only inside the two-word every one, since the solid compound everyone admits nothing between its halves — ✗every last everyone, ✗everylast one — which is one more reminder that everyone and every one are different words.
entries.see also: every one, each, all, not one, not a one, none, everyone, every last (determiner), every single (determiner), each and every (determiner)

entries.meaning: Covers every member of a group without exception, and unlike everyone it can point at objects.
examples: Every one of the smoke detectors was dead.
She has read every one of his novels.
We ordered a dozen, and every one arrived broken.
Every one of them has to be signed in blue ink.
I checked the receipts, and every single one was from the same store.
Not every one of the complaints was justified.
entries.pronunciation note: two words, with the main stress on one. Compare the solid compound everyone /ˈɛvriwʌn/ · EV-ree-wun, stressed on the first syllable.
entries.русский: каждый; все до одного — раздельно, также и о вещах, в отличие от everyone
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the pronoun that stands in for the determiner every, which has no pronoun form of its own
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: every member of a definite set — things as well as people, which is the point of it, since the one-word everyone refers to people only. Countables only.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Every one of the bulbs was burned out; Every one of them has to be signed. Referring back, singular they is standard: Every one of the drivers renewed their license.
entries.pattern: every one of [determiner + plural noun] · every one of [object pronoun] · every one standing alone (I've read every one) · every single one (emphatic) · not every one (partial negation) · almost / nearly every one
entries.the test: if you can insert single — every single one — it is two words. Against each: every one stresses that the sweep is complete, each that the members are separate; both take singular verbs, and every one accepts almost and nearly while each does not.
entries.contrast: This entry exists because every has no pronoun use at all. ✗Every was accounted for is ungrammatical; the pronoun is every one, two words. Written solid, everyone is a compound indefinite pronoun that refers only to people and never takes of: ✗everyone of them is a spelling error for every one of them. Both take a singular verb, as every compound indefinite does — everyone is, somebody was, nobody has — while the pronoun referring back to them is normally singular they.
entries.see also: each, all, one, none, everyone, everything, every (determiner)

entries.meaning: Rejects both members of a pair at once — the negative counterpart of both.
examples: Neither of the candidates was willing to debate.
I tried both keys, and neither worked.
Neither of us had eaten since breakfast.
She looked at the two offers; neither was serious.
Neither of those explanations accounts for the noise.
He apologized to neither of them.
Which one do you want? — Neither, thanks.
entries.pronunciation note: /i/ dominant in American English
entries.русский: ни тот ни другой — ни один из ровно двух; при трёх и более — none
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: negative distributive pronoun (also a determiner, neither side, half of the correlative neither … nor, and an adverb of negative agreement, Neither do I)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: not one and not the other of exactly two — people or things, countables only. With three or more it is wrong: ✗neither of the three; use none.
entries.agreement: singular — Neither of the answers is correct; Neither was available. Plural verbs (Neither of them were) are frequent in speech and have a long history, but this is the one place in the group where a conservative editor reliably objects, and the singular is correct in every register. Referring back, singular they is standard: Neither of the drivers admitted they were at fault.
entries.pattern: neither of [determiner + plural noun] + singular verb · neither of [object pronoun] · neither [singular verb] · [verb] neither · standing alone as an answer (Neither, thanks) · neither … nor (correlative conjunction, a different use) · Neither do I, Neither am I (adverb, with inversion)
entries.one negative to a clause in edited writi: ✗I don't want neither is nonstandard in standard American English. It is not carelessness — negative concord is regular and systematic in African American English and in Southern and Appalachian vernacular, where it is how negation is built — but it is stigmatized in every kind of formal writing, so write I don't want either or I want neither. Against none: neither for a set of two, none for three or more or for a mass. Against nor: nor is the conjunction (neither fish nor fowl) and cannot stand in for this pronoun.
entries.contrast: Neither is the negative of either and, like it, is limited to two.
entries.see also: either, both, none, each, nobody, neither (determiner)

entries.meaning: One of two, when the two are all there is. ---
examples: You can't have both — it's one or the other.
One or the other of them has been leaving the gate open.
Either he apologizes or she does; one or the other has to move first.
The noise is the compressor or the fan, one or the other.
We can afford the roof or the furnace, and I would take one or the other over neither.
One or the other of those two dates is going to work.
entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to /ɚ/ and the before the vowel of other is /ði/, so the four words run together with the stress on other
entries.русский: тот или другой, одно из двух — из ровно двух известных вариантов
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: distributive pronoun phrase — the positive counterpart of neither, over a set of exactly two
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: one of exactly two already-identified alternatives, with a commitment that it is one of them and none as to which. People or things, countables only. With three or more it is wrong: ✗one or the other of the five; the phrase is one of them or any of them.
entries.agreement: singular — One or the other is going to have to give; One or the other of the tenants has been feeding it.
entries.pattern: one or the other [singular verb] · one or the other of [determiner + plural noun] · one or the other of [object pronoun] · [verb] one or the other · it has to be one or the other · one way or the other (an adverbial, not this pronoun)
entries.contrast: Against either: either leaves the choice genuinely open and often means that both would do (Either works for me), while one or the other insists that a choice must be made and that there is no third option (It has to be one or the other). Against neither: the negative over the same pair. Against another: that adds a further item to an open set, where this phrase closes the set at two — which is what the definite the other inside it is doing, and why the phrase cannot be stretched past two.
entries.see also: either, neither, both, other, another, each, one, one or two (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points at an unspecified part of a group or quantity — in the non-assertive contexts, at a part whose existence is in question.
examples: I looked for eggs, but there weren't any.
Have any of them replied yet?
If any of this sounds familiar, say so now.
She wanted advice, and I didn't have any to give.
Pick a card — any will do.
Any of these routes gets you downtown by seven.

senses.head: Non-assertive: in negatives, questions, and conditionals
examples: I looked for eggs, but there weren't any.
Have any of them replied yet?
If any of this sounds familiar, say so now.
She wanted advice, and I didn't have any to give.

senses.head: Free choice: no matter which one
examples: Pick a card — any will do.
Any of these routes gets you downtown by seven.

entries.pronunciation note: regionally /ˈɪni/ · IN-ee in Southern and South Midland speech; the word resists reduction even when unstressed
entries.русский: какой-нибудь, сколько-нибудь; никакой — форма вместо some в отрицаниях, вопросах, условиях
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: non-assertive quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, any milk, and an adverb of degree, any better)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: an unspecified member, members, or amount of a set — countables (people or things) or a mass. It is the word that appears where some cannot: in negatives, questions, conditionals, and after words carrying negative force (hardly, without, refuse, doubt).
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to. Plural countable referent → plural verb, and this is the default: Are any of the seats still free? Mass referent → singular: Is any of the soup left? The singular also appears with a plural of-phrase when the sense is "any single one" — If any of these excuses is true, I'll be amazed — and both numbers are standard there.
entries.pattern: any of [determiner + noun] · any of [object pronoun] · any [verb] · [negative] + [verb] + any (I don't have any) · [question] + any · if + any · hardly any, scarcely any, not any
entries.contrast: Any vs. some. Some is assertive and belongs in plain statements; any is non-assertive and belongs in negatives, questions, and conditionals: I have some / I don't have any / Do you have any? The two exceptions are worth knowing: some appears in a question when you expect or are inviting a yes (Would you like some?), and any appears in a plain statement when it means free choice, "no matter which" (Any of them will do). Not any is equivalent to none: I didn't buy any = I bought none. Before a bare noun any is a determiner (any milk); alone or with of, a pronoun.
entries.see also: some, none, either, enough, anyone, anything, any (determiner)

entries.meaning: Any item at all from the list just given.
examples: Check the box if any of the above apply to you.
Damage caused by any of the above is excluded from coverage.
He denied that any of the above had ever been discussed.
If any of the above is unclear, ask before you sign.
The grant is void if the applicant fails any of the above.
Symptoms may include fever, rash, or joint pain; call your doctor if you develop any of the above.
entries.pronunciation note: the of reduces to /əv/ or /ə/, and the before the vowel of above is /ði/
entries.русский: любое из вышеперечисленного — язык бланков, инструкций, гарантий, спецификаций
entries.register: neutral — the language of forms, instructions, warranties, and specifications
entries.type: non-assertive quantifying pronoun phrase, deictic
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: any item at all from a list just given. Both the non-assertive any of negatives and questions and the free-choice any of "no matter which" apply to it, and its antecedent is textual — lines on a page rather than things in the world.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — If any of the above apply, call the office (the listed conditions, plural, and the ordinary case) and If any of the above is true, stop here (any single one, singular) are both standard, exactly as under any.
entries.pattern: if any of the above [verb] · [negative] + [verb] + any of the above · [verb] any of the above · any of the above + relative clause · standing alone on a checklist
entries.contrast: Against all of the above and none of the above: one list, three quantities. Against bare any: the antecedent is the whole difference — any of them points at things already in the conversation, any of the above at lines on the page, which makes the phrase almost unusable in speech and hard to do without on a form. The above is a noun here, so ✗any of above is not English.
entries.see also: all of the above, none of the above, any, any one, some, either, any (determiner)

entries.meaning: Any single member of a set, people or things alike.
examples: Any one of these keys should open the shed.
The chain will break at any one of a dozen weak points.
Any one of them could have made the call.
Losing any one of the three would sink the deal.
Take any one and leave the rest for the next shift.
The failure of any one of the pumps shuts down the whole line.
entries.pronunciation note: two words, with the main stress on one; compare the solid compound anyone /ˈɛniwʌn/ · EN-ee-wun, stressed on the first syllable
entries.русский: любой один, какой-нибудь один — раздельно, также и о вещах, в отличие от anyone
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the singular-picking counterpart of the determiner any, and the partner of every one
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: a single unspecified member of a set — things as well as people, which is the point of the two-word spelling, since the one-word anyone covers people only. Countables only: ✗any one of the water.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Any one of the fuses is enough to trip it; Any one of them was capable of it. Referring back, singular they is standard: Any one of the drivers could have left their lights on.
entries.pattern: any one of [determiner + plural noun] · any one of [object pronoun] · any one standing alone (Take any one) · any single one (emphatic) · at any one time, no more than any one (determiner uses, not this pronoun)
entries.contrast: The spelling is the meaning. Written solid, anyone refers to people only and never takes of — ✗anyone of them is a misspelling of any one of them. Written as two words, any one takes of freely and points at objects as readily as at people. The test is the one that separates everyone from every one: if you can insert single, it is two words. Against either: either is limited to a set of two, any one wants three or more. Against every one: the same shape and the opposite quantity — one member against all of them.
entries.see also: every one, any, any of the above, one, either, none, anyone, anything, any (determiner)

entries.meaning: Some particular members of a group, unnamed on purpose.
examples: Certain of the trustees have asked to see the accounts.
Certain of them were never told the meeting had moved.
The report is sharply critical of certain of the practices it describes.
Certain of the older tenants remember when the building had a doorman.
She declined to name certain of the parties involved.
Certain of the documents had been removed before the audit began.
entries.pronunciation note: the second syllable is a syllabic /n/ with no vowel of its own and the /t/ is usually a glottal stop, so the word comes out as two beats, SUR-'n
entries.русский: некоторые, определённые — книжн., о намеренно не названных лицах или вещах
entries.register: formal and literary — reports, minutes, and legal prose; the everyday word for the same quantity is some
entries.type: quantifying pronoun, partitive only — it lives in the frame certain of + noun phrase and nowhere else (also a determiner, certain people, and the adjective of confidence, I'm certain)
entries.person / number: third person; plural
entries.refers to: some particular but deliberately unnamed members of a set of countables — people or things — with the implication that the writer knows which ones and is declining to say. Never a mass: ✗certain of the water.
entries.agreement: plural — Certain of the members have objected; Certain of them were never informed.
entries.pattern: certain of [determiner + plural noun] · certain of [object pronoun] · and nothing else — bare ✗Certain refused and ✗I spoke to certain are impossible, so unlike some and most this pronoun can never stand alone
entries.contrast: Against some: the plain word for the same quantity, at home in every register and in every frame; certain of adds formality and a note of discretion. Against the determiner certain: in front of a noun the word is a determiner (certain irregularities, a certain reluctance) and belongs to the determiner dictionary — the pronoun exists only after of. And keep both apart from the adjective certain meaning sure (I am certain of it), which also takes of: the giveaway is that the adjective has a personal subject and can be graded (more certain, quite certain), while the pronoun can do neither.
entries.see also: some, several, a few, others, most, certain (determiner), a certain (determiner)

entries.meaning: Names the amount or number that is sufficient for a purpose — no more and no less.
examples: There's coffee left, but not enough for four people.
I've had enough of the excuses.
Buy two boxes — one isn't enough.
Enough of them showed up to hold the vote.
Enough is enough.
She had saved enough to cover the deposit.
entries.pronunciation note: the first vowel is a schwa in ordinary speech and can drop entirely in the fixed phrase 'nough said
entries.русский: достаточно, довольно — достаточное количество или число
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, enough chairs, and an adverb that follows what it modifies, warm enough)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular with a mass and plural with countables
entries.refers to: a sufficient amount of a mass or a sufficient number of countables; also, in the idiom I've had enough, an abstract quantity of a situation.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — Enough of the money is left to cover rent (mass, singular); Enough of the volunteers have shown up to hold the vote (countable, plural). The fixed sentence Enough is enough is singular.
entries.pattern: enough [verb] · enough of [determiner + noun] · enough of [object pronoun] · [verb] enough (I've had enough) · enough to [infinitive] · more than enough, not nearly enough, quite enough
entries.the position trap: as a determiner enough goes before the noun (enough chairs), but as an adverb it goes after the adjective (warm enough, ✗enough warm) — this is the most common error with the word, and it is not a pronoun error at all.
entries.contrast: Against plenty: enough is exactly the amount needed and claims nothing beyond it; plenty is comfortably more than needed. The of is obligatory before a determiner or pronoun (enough of the cake, enough of them, ✗enough them), and bare enough is used when the referent is already understood.
entries.see also: plenty, a lot, much, many, more, enough (determiner)

entries.meaning: At least one, with the count deliberately left open — the phrase a drafter writes to keep a rule true either way.
examples: One or more of the following documents must be attached to the application.
The policy is void if one or more of the conditions are not met.
One or more of them had clearly read the file before the hearing.
Check the box if one or more of the above apply to you.
Applicants may be interviewed by one or more of the committee members.
The statute takes effect whenever one or more of the parties resides in the state.
entries.pronunciation note: or reduces to /ɚ/ and never carries stress, so the three words come out in two beats
entries.русский: один или несколько — юр. и тех.: «не менее одного»; в речи at least one
entries.register: formal and technical — statutes, regulations, contracts, standards, forms, and specifications; ordinary speech says at least one or some
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — a disjunction of one and more used as a single indefinite quantity
entries.person / number: third person; construes singular or plural, with the plural the ordinary choice
entries.refers to: at least one member of a set of countables, with no upper bound — things or people. Never a mass: ✗one or more of the water. Its whole reason for existing is to keep a rule true whether the count turns out to be one or twenty.
entries.agreement: either, and the verb follows the nearer conjunct. One or more of the following apply is the ordinary form and the one standards and statutes print, because more is the conjunct next to the verb; One or more of the following applies, agreeing with one, is also standard and is common in older drafting. American editors accept both, and the plural is the safer default.
entries.pattern: one or more [verb] · one or more of [determiner + plural noun] · one or more of [object pronoun] · [verb] one or more · one or more of the following · the parallel two or more, three or more, one or two
entries.contrast: Against any: any leaves the existence of the thing open (if any of them apply), while one or more asserts that at least one does. Against some: the everyday word, vaguer, and unusable in a rule that has to be exact. Against at least one: the same meaning in plainer English, and what a plain-language editor substitutes. Against bare one: that commits to exactly one, which is precisely the commitment this phrase is drafted to avoid. Because it is drafting language it belongs where drafting language belongs, and never in narrative or conversation — one or more of us was hungry is a joke, not a sentence.
entries.see also: any one, any, some, several, one, two, any of the above, one or more (determiner), one or two (determiner)

entries.ipa: /sʌm/ stressed, weak /səm/ and in fast speech syllabic /sm̩/
entries.meaning: Names an unspecified part of a larger set or quantity, without saying which part or how much.
examples: Some of the windows were painted shut.
There's soup on the stove if you want some.
Some of the evidence was thrown out before trial.
He kept some and gave the rest away.
Some arrived early; others never showed up at all.
Some say the road was never meant to be finished.

senses.head: An unspecified part or number of something
examples: Some of the windows were painted shut.
There's soup on the stove if you want some.
Some of the evidence was thrown out before trial.

senses.head: Contrasted with the rest
body: Often paired with others or the rest.
examples: He kept some and gave the rest away.
Some arrived early; others never showed up at all.

senses.head: People in general, as a bare subject
body: Formal in tone, common in journalism.
examples: Some say the road was never meant to be finished.

entries.pronunciation note: some of them runs together as /ˈsʌməvəm/ · SUM-uh-vum
entries.русский: некоторые, часть, некоторое количество — в утвердительных предложениях
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: assertive quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, some milk, and an informal adverb of degree, she slept some)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: an unspecified part of a set or quantity — countable things or people (plural), or a mass (singular). Bare some as a subject can also refer to people in general, as in Some say it was never finished.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — Some of the chairs are broken (countable → plural); Some of the paint is dry (mass → singular). This is the same rule that governs all, any, most, more, and none: with these the of-phrase decides the number, not the pronoun.
entries.pattern: some of [determiner + noun] · some of [object pronoun] · some [verb] (Some disagree) · [verb] some (I'd like some) · some … others … · some more, and some
entries.contrast: Some vs. any — some in statements and in offers or requests where you expect a yes (Would you like some?), any in negatives, questions, and conditionals. Against a few and a little: some is neutral about how much, a few commits to a small count, a little to a small amount. Stressed /sʌm/ some means "certain ones as opposed to others" (Some of us disagree); unstressed /səm/ it just means an unspecified part. Before a bare noun some is a determiner, not this pronoun.
entries.see also: any, all, most, none, others, a few, someone, something, some (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large quantity, exaggerated out loud, and the one member of the -load family that is safe to print anywhere.
examples: They spent a boatload on lawyers before the case ever reached trial.
A boatload of them arrived damaged and had to be sent back.
She knows a boatload about municipal bonds and says almost nothing about it.
We got a boatload of complaints the week the new machine went in.
A boatload of the paperwork turned out to be duplicates.
He promised a boatload and delivered a folder.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/, and the /t/ is unreleased or glottal before the /l/, so the word comes out in two beats with the stress on the first
entries.русский: куча, вагон — разг., но не бранное; о большом количестве
entries.register: informal but not vulgar — the printable member of the -load family, at home in speech, in journalism, and in casual writing
entries.type: hyperbolic quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a boatload of money, and the literal count noun, a boatload of gravel)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass, stated as open exaggeration — money, work, trouble, complaints, people.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — A boatload of them were returned (countable → plural); A boatload of the money was never accounted for (mass → singular). The literal cargo behaves like any other count noun and stays singular: A boatload of gravel was delivered Tuesday.
entries.pattern: a boatload [verb] · a boatload of [determiner + noun] · a boatload of [object pronoun] · [verb] a boatload (They made a boatload) · a whole boatload, boatloads of
entries.variants: a truckload, a busload, a carload, a trainload, and the plural boatloads; the same frame with a rude noun in it gives a shitload and its minced relatives
entries.contrast: Against a shitload: the identical construction with the vulgarity taken out, which is exactly what it is for — an American who wants that much force in a sentence a client, a professor, or a stranger will read writes a boatload. Against a ton and tons: interchangeable in sense, with a boatload the more visual of them. Against a lot: the plain word, and the one to use when no exaggeration is wanted. In formal writing all of them go to a great deal, many, or a large number. And note the adverbial gap: thanks a ton is fixed and ✗thanks a boatload is not idiomatic.
entries.see also: a shitload, a slew, a ton, tons, a lot, a bunch, gobs, scads, a shitload of (determiner), tons of (determiner)

entries.meaning: The casual word for a fair number of things, or a fair amount of one.
examples: We ordered too much and had a bunch left over.
A bunch of them showed up without tickets.
She asked me to bring chairs, so I brought a bunch.
A bunch of the paperwork was still sitting in his inbox.
I had a bunch to say and no chance to say it.
Of the twenty who signed up, a bunch never came back.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and never stressed; before of the phrase runs together, a bunch of them /əˈbʌntʃəvəm/ · uh-BUN-chuh-vum
entries.русский: куча, кучка, полно — разг., неопределённо большое количество
entries.register: informal — casual speech and casual writing; an editor replaces it with several, many, or a number of
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a bunch of questions, and an ordinary count noun, a bunch of grapes)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: an indefinite largish number of countable things or people, or amount of a mass — work, money, trouble. The literal cluster tied or grown together (a bunch of bananas) is the count noun, not this pronoun.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — A bunch of them were late (countable → plural); A bunch of the paint was ruined (mass → singular). The count noun goes the other way and stays singular: That bunch of grapes is overripe.
entries.pattern: a bunch [verb] · a bunch of [determiner + noun] · a bunch of [object pronoun] · [verb] a bunch (I bought a bunch) · a whole bunch, a bunch more · adverbial thanks a bunch
entries.contrast: Against a lot: the same job one notch more casual, and still faintly conscious of its origin in things gathered together, so it sits more comfortably with countables than with abstractions. Against several and a number of: what a copy editor puts in its place. Thanks a bunch is an adverbial and is more often sarcastic than grateful; bunches is the count noun and not this pronoun. Note the difference the article makes: a bunch of us is several of us, the bunch of us is all of us.
entries.see also: a lot, lots, a ton, tons, loads, several, many, plenty, a bunch of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large number of countable things, offered as more than the listener probably expects.
examples: A good many of the original tenants are still in the building.
Of the promises made that spring, a good many were quietly dropped.
He has a good many of them stored out in the garage.
A good many would disagree with you about that.
She interviewed sixty people and found a good many who remembered the fire.
A good many of us had never flown before that morning.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/, good keeps a light secondary beat, and the main stress falls on many, whose vowel is /ɛ/ and not /æ/
entries.русский: немало, изрядное число — слегка книжн.; только о счётных, для массы a good deal
entries.register: neutral, with a faintly bookish and older-American flavor; the everyday equivalents are a lot and quite a few
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — many with a degree word fused in front of it (also a determiner, a good many years)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a large number of countable things or people — more than several, and offered as more than the listener would guess. Never a mass: ✗a good many of the water; the mass counterpart is a good deal.
entries.agreement: plural, always — A good many were turned away; A good many of the houses have been rebuilt. The indefinite article at the front changes nothing, because the head of the phrase is many, and there is no singular use at all.
entries.pattern: a good many [plural verb] · a good many of [determiner + plural noun] · a good many of [object pronoun] · [verb] a good many · the determiner a good many + plural noun (a good many years) · the stronger a great many
entries.variants: a great many (stronger and more formal), the regional a fair many, and the mass counterparts a good deal and a great deal
entries.contrast: Against bare many: many is neutral and slightly formal as a bare subject, while a good many reads as a considered estimate — it says "more than you would think," which is why it so often follows a concession. Against quite a few: nearly the same quantity and the same effect, one notch more casual. Against a good deal: the mass twin, and the count/mass line between them is absolute — a good many of the years but a good deal of the time. The article cannot be dropped: ✗good many of them came.
entries.see also: many, quite a few, a great deal, a lot, several, a few, most, a good many (determiner), a great many (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large amount of something measured rather than counted, said a register above a lot.
examples: A great deal has changed since the last inspection.
A great deal of the money is still unaccounted for.
She knows a great deal about eighteenth-century printing.
He promised a great deal and delivered almost none of it.
Of the evidence collected that night, a great deal was later ruled inadmissible.
They spent a great deal of it on lawyers before the case ever reached trial.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and never stressed, and the /t/ of great is normally unreleased or glottal before the /d/, so the phrase comes out as two beats, uh-gray(t)-DEEL
entries.русский: очень много, масса — только о неисчисляемом; нейтр.-книжн.
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a great deal of money, and an adverb of degree, she travels a great deal)
entries.person / number: third person; singular, always — the mass counterpart of a lot, and no plural sense is open to it
entries.refers to: a large amount of a mass or an abstraction — work, time, money, trouble, attention, knowledge. Never countable things: ✗a great deal of the chairs, ✗A great deal of them were returned; for countables the words are many, a lot, and a good many.
entries.agreement: singular, always — A great deal has changed since then; A great deal of the money is still unaccounted for. The head of the phrase is the noun deal, so no plural inside the of-phrase can pull the verb over: ✗A great deal of the evidence were ruled inadmissible.
entries.pattern: a great deal [singular verb] · a great deal of [determiner + mass noun] · a great deal of [it / this / that] · [verb] a great deal (He knows a great deal) · a great deal more, a great deal less (degree modifier) · the variants a good deal and, informally, quite a bit
entries.contrast: Against a lot and lots: the three mean the same thing and differ in register only — lots is casual, a lot is everyday, a great deal is the formal one, and it is what the a lot, lots, and much entries send you to when the writing has to be edited upward. Against much: the two overlap in the mass slot, but bare much is stilted in a plain positive statement (✗We have much) exactly where a great deal is ordinary (We have a great deal to discuss). Against many: the count/mass line is absolute — a great deal of work but many jobs, and ✗a great deal of people is an error, not a stylistic choice. Before a pronoun or a determiner the of is obligatory (a great deal of it, a great deal of the money, ✗a great deal it); bare a great deal is used only when the referent is already understood. Keep the phrase apart from the ordinary count noun deal (a good deal on a car, the deal fell through, two deals), which pluralizes and has nothing to do with quantity.
entries.see also: a lot, lots, much, plenty, more, little, a great deal of (determiner)

entries.meaning: The everyday word for a large quantity, whether counted or measured.
examples: We invited thirty people, and a lot showed up.
A lot of the paperwork is still sitting on his desk.
She had savings once, but not a lot.
A lot of them were returned unopened.
A lot has changed since you were here last.
Of the original crew, a lot had already quit by June.
entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ is usually flapped or cut off in speech. Always two words: ✗alot is a misspelling, never a variant.
entries.русский: много, куча — обычное разговорное «много», и о счётных, и о массе
entries.register: informal to neutral; avoid in formal writing
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a lot of money, and an adverb, she reads a lot)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass — things, people, or abstractions. It is the word American English actually uses in positive statements where much and many would sound stiff.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — A lot of the students are commuters (countable → plural); A lot of the work is already done (mass → singular). Bare A lot has changed is singular because the referent is an unspecified mass of things.
entries.pattern: a lot [verb] · a lot of [determiner + noun] · a lot of [object pronoun] · [verb] a lot · quite a lot, an awful lot, a whole lot · a lot more, a lot less
entries.contrast: Against much and many: in a plain positive statement, a lot is the natural choice and much is nearly impossible (I ate a lot, ✗I ate much), while much and many are perfectly natural in negatives and questions (I didn't eat much, How many are left?). Against lots: same meaning, same agreement, one notch more casual. In formal writing replace all three with many, much, a great deal, or a large number. Note the spelling once more: two words.
entries.see also: lots, a great deal, many, much, plenty, most, enough, a lot of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large quantity, said with a swear word in it for emphasis.
examples: They spent a shitload on the renovation and still can't sell the place.
A shitload of them showed up without tickets.
She knows a shitload about early punk labels.
We had a shitload of trouble getting the permit signed.
A shitload of the wiring had to be pulled out and replaced.
He promised a shitload and delivered almost nothing.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/, and the /t/ is unreleased or glottal before the /l/, so the word comes out in two beats with the stress on the first
entries.русский: груб.: дохрена, до хрена — количество то же, что у a lot, грубость лишь усиливает
entries.register: vulgar slang — casual speech among people who already swear in front of one another, and writing that is imitating it. Never in a cover letter, a client email, a court filing, a paper, a press release, or anything a stranger will read; the printable substitutes are a boatload, a ton, and a lot.
