entries.type: vulgar hyperbolic quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a shitload of money)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass — money, work, trouble, time, people. The vulgarity carries emphasis and nothing else: the quantity named is exactly the quantity a lot names.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — A shitload of them were returned (countable → plural); A shitload of the money was gone (mass → singular). The plural shitloads behaves the same way.
entries.pattern: a shitload [verb] · a shitload of [determiner + noun] · a shitload of [object pronoun] · [verb] a shitload (They made a shitload) · a whole shitload, shitloads of · adverbial a shitload better
entries.variants: the minced a crapload and a buttload, mild enough to print in more places; the intensified a shit ton and a fuckton, the second of which is stronger than this entry and not weaker; and the entirely clean a boatload, a truckload, and a busload, dictionaried at a boatload
entries.contrast: Against the vulgar minimizers squat, diddly-squat, and jack shit: the same register aimed the other way, and grammatically a different animal — He knows squat already means "he knows nothing" with no negative word anywhere in the sentence, while a shitload has no such negative-polarity behavior and simply means "a large amount." Against a boatload: the same construction with the vulgarity removed, and the usual repair when the sentence has to be shown to somebody. Against a lot and tons: the neutral and the merely informal members of the family. Nothing but force is lost in the substitution, which is worth knowing, because nothing about the word makes it more precise than a lot.
entries.see also: a boatload, a slew, gobs, scads, a ton, tons, a lot, diddly, diddly-squat, squat, jack, jack shit, a shitload of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large batch of countable things arriving together, usually as a problem.
examples: A slew of complaints came in the week the new hours took effect.
The bill drew a slew of amendments before it ever reached the floor.
Of the applications filed that month, a slew were missing signatures.
She has a slew of them stacked on the passenger seat.
A slew of injuries kept the team out of the playoffs.
He answered two questions and dodged a slew of others.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/; the noun is a homophone of the past tense slew of slay and of the slough that means a swamp, and it is related to neither — it comes from Irish sluagh, a crowd
entries.русский: целая куча, вал — амер., обычно о неприятном потоке счётных вещей
entries.register: informal to neutral and distinctly American — ordinary in speech and in journalism, and mild enough that copy editors often leave it alone
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a slew of complaints)
entries.person / number: third person; plural
entries.refers to: a large and usually unwelcome number of countable things or people arriving together — complaints, lawsuits, injuries, amendments, applicants, errors. Never a mass: ✗a slew of the money.
entries.agreement: plural — A slew of them were rejected; A slew of complaints have come in since Friday. The singular A slew of complaints has come in, treating the batch as one arrival, also occurs and is unobjectionable; the plural is much the commoner.
entries.pattern: a slew of [determiner + plural noun] · a slew of [object pronoun] · a slew [plural verb] · [verb] a slew · a whole slew of
entries.contrast: Against a bunch and a lot: the same size with a different attitude — a slew arrives all at once and is usually a problem, which is why journalists reach for it in front of complaints, injuries, and lawsuits. Against several and a number of: the neutral words, and what an editor substitutes when the tone has to come down. Against a shitload: the same job with no vulgarity attached. Bare a slew as a subject is rare and strained; the phrase wants its of-phrase.
entries.see also: a bunch, a boatload, a shitload, a lot, several, many, scads, gobs, a slew of (determiner)

entries.meaning: The everyday American exaggeration for a large quantity.
examples: There's a ton left if you want seconds.
A ton of them never bothered to reply.
She knows a ton about early jazz recordings.
We had a ton of trouble getting the permit.
Of the files he asked for, a ton had already been destroyed.
He promised a ton and delivered almost nothing.
entries.pronunciation note: the article reduces to /ə/; the vowel is the one in sun, never the one in tone
entries.русский: куча, море, вагон — разг. преувеличение, и о счётных, и о массе
entries.register: informal — everyday American speech and casual writing; out of place in formal prose
entries.type: hyperbolic quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a ton of work, an adverb, it helped a ton, and the unit of weight)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass, stated as open exaggeration — things, people, work, money, time.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — A ton of them were returned (countable → plural); A ton of the work is already done (mass → singular). The literal weight behaves like any other count noun: A ton of gravel was delivered, three tons were ordered.
entries.pattern: a ton [verb] · a ton of [determiner + noun] · a ton of [object pronoun] · [verb] a ton (She knows a ton) · a whole ton, a ton more · adverbial thanks a ton, it helped a ton
entries.contrast: Against a lot: the same meaning with the volume up — a ton is heard as hyperbole and a lot is not. Against tons: identical in sense and in agreement, and the plural is the commoner of the two before of, while the singular is the form that survives in the fixed adverbials. In formal writing all of them go to a great deal, many, or a large number. Keep the pronoun apart from the unit of weight: a ton of gravel can be either, and only the context says whether anybody weighed it.
entries.see also: tons, a lot, lots, loads, heaps, oodles, a bunch, a great deal, tons of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large quantity, in an American colloquialism that leans toward money.
examples: They made gobs on the first two records and nothing at all after that.
There's gobs of room in the back if you want to stretch out.
Gobs of them were handed out free at the entrance.
She has time, and gobs of it, now that the store has closed.
Gobs of the money never reached the program it was raised for.
We asked for a little help and got gobs.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; one syllable, with the vowel of rob
entries.русский: уйма, куча — амер. разг., чуть простонародно и старомодно; чаще о деньгах
entries.register: informal and American — casual speech and casual writing, faintly folksy and faintly dated; not for formal prose
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, gobs of money, and an ordinary count noun, two gobs of glue)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large amount of a mass or a large number of countables — money above all, and time, room, and trouble. The quantifier has no singular: a gob is a lump of something, not a quantity.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent, not with the -s — Gobs of them were given away (countable → plural); Gobs of money was spent on it (mass → singular), where the plural were spent is also heard and unobjectionable. The literal count noun keeps a real plural: Two gobs of glue were holding it together.
entries.pattern: gobs of [determiner + noun] · gobs of [object pronoun] · [verb] gobs (They made gobs) · there are gobs left · gobs more
entries.contrast: Against scads: the nearest relative, and the two are interchangeable in practice, with gobs leaning toward money and mass quantities and scads toward things you count. Against oodles: playful where gobs is merely casual. Against tons and loads: the unmarked informal words, and the ones a reader will not notice at all. In formal writing every one of them goes to a great deal, many, or a large number. Keep the quantifier apart from the count noun a gob — a lump of glue, wax, or spit — and from British slang gob meaning mouth, which is a different word entirely.
entries.see also: scads, oodles, tons, loads, heaps, lots, a boatload, oodles of (determiner), a mess of (determiner)

entries.meaning: The British and Australian word for a large quantity, counted or measured.
examples: Don't rush — we have heaps of time.
Heaps of them had already been sold by the time we arrived.
There's heaps left in the pot.
She's got money, and heaps of it.
Heaps of the seats were still empty at kickoff.
I asked for a few and got heaps.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form
entries.русский: уйма, куча — разг., преим. брит., австрал. и новозел.
entries.register: informal, and chiefly British, Australian, and New Zealand; an American meets it in imported writing and television rather than in native speech, where tons and loads fill the slot
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, heaps of time, and an informal adverb, heaps better)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass — things, people, time, money, room.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent, not with the -s — Heaps of them were sold (countable → plural); Heaps of the food was thrown out (mass → singular). The ordinary count noun keeps a real plural, and there the -s does count: The heaps of gravel were in the way.
entries.pattern: heaps of [determiner + noun] · heaps of [object pronoun] · [verb] heaps (We have heaps) · there are heaps left · heaps more · adverbial heaps better, thanks heaps
entries.contrast: Against loads: the two behave identically and both are British in origin, but loads has crossed into American speech and heaps has not, which makes heaps the more strongly marked of the pair for an American ear. Against tons and a ton: the native American equivalents. Against the singular a heap: American English keeps that mainly in the Southern a heap of trouble; the separate heap big is a stereotyped imitation of Native American speech, is offensive, and is best left alone entirely. In formal writing the word is a great deal or many.
entries.see also: loads, tons, a ton, lots, a lot, oodles, plenty, heaps of (determiner), a heap of (determiner)

entries.meaning: An indefinite large number, pitched at an order of magnitude rather than counted.
examples: Hundreds were turned away at the gate before the doors even opened.
Hundreds of the letters were never opened.
The city printed ten thousand ballots and spoiled hundreds.
Thousands of them are still in circulation.
Of the birds banded that spring, dozens were recovered within the year.
Millions have been spent on a study nobody has read.
entries.pronunciation note: the /d/ inside the cluster is regularly lost in casual American speech, which is why the careless spelling hunderds keeps turning up
entries.русский: сотни — неопределённо большое число счётных; о массе не говорят
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun — the plural of the numeral noun hundred used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, hundreds of letters)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: an indefinite large number of countable things or people, in the range the word names and usually well past it — the point of the plural is that nobody counted. Never a mass: ✗hundreds of the water.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Hundreds were turned away at the gate; Hundreds of the letters have never been opened. So is the exact numeral (Two hundred were counted), which is why the difference between them is one of meaning and not of grammar.
entries.pattern: hundreds [plural verb] · hundreds of [determiner + plural noun] · hundreds of [object pronoun] · [verb] hundreds · hundreds upon hundreds, hundreds and hundreds · in the hundreds, by the hundreds · the ladder dozens, scores, hundreds, thousands, millions, billions
entries.variants: dozens, scores, thousands, millions, billions, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands — the same construction and the same grammar throughout, differing only in the size claimed
entries.contrast: The -s is what makes it vague. Two hundred is a count, hundreds is an estimate, and the plural is the whole difference; the same holds for a dozen against dozens and a thousand against thousands. Against many and a lot: those name a large number without committing to an order of magnitude, while hundreds commits and can therefore be wrong — a reader who learns that forty people were turned away will hold hundreds against you. Against countless and innumerable: those refuse the count outright. And the of is obligatory in front of a determiner or a pronoun: hundreds of the letters, hundreds of them, ✗hundreds them.
entries.see also: two, many, a lot, a good many, most, several, hundreds of (determiner), thousands of (determiner), millions of (determiner), dozens of (determiner), scores of (determiner)

entries.meaning: The casual word, British by birth and now American too, for a large quantity.
examples: Don't worry about chairs — we have loads.
Loads of them had already left by ten.
There's loads left if you're still hungry.
She has time, and loads of it.
Loads of the paperwork turned out to be duplicates.
I asked for a couple of examples and got loads.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form
entries.русский: уйма, полно — разг., по происхождению брит., но обычно и в амер. речи
entries.register: informal; British in origin and now ordinary in casual American speech and writing, though still a shade more British-sounding than tons
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, loads of time, and an informal adverb, loads better)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass — things, people, time, money, work.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent, not with the -s — Loads of people are coming (countable → plural); Loads of the wiring was corroded (mass → singular). The ordinary count noun keeps a real plural: Two loads of laundry were still in the machine.
entries.pattern: loads of [determiner + noun] · loads of [object pronoun] · [verb] loads (We have loads) · there are loads left · loads more · adverbial loads better, thanks loads
entries.contrast: Against lots: same meaning, same agreement, same register, and the two are interchangeable — lots is the American default and loads the British one. Against heaps: the same British pattern, except that loads has crossed the Atlantic and heaps has not. Like lots, loads is awkward as a bare subject: Loads were left over is possible but strained, and There were loads left over is what people actually say. In formal writing the words are many, much, and a great deal.
entries.see also: lots, a lot, tons, a ton, heaps, oodles, plenty, loads of (determiner)

entries.meaning: The casual word for a great deal or a great many.
examples: Don't worry about paper — we have lots.
Lots of them had already been claimed by noon.
Lots of the wiring was corroded.
She's got money, and lots of it.
I asked for a few examples and got lots.
There were lots left over after the sale.
entries.русский: много, полно — разг., только в непринуждённой речи и письме
entries.register: informal — colloquial speech and casual writing only
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, lots of time)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass. Things, people, or abstractions.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent, not with the -s — Lots of the food was wasted (mass → singular); Lots of people are coming (countable → plural). The plural-looking ending has no effect on the verb, which is what separates it from the ordinary count noun lots (the parking lots were full), where the plural is real.
entries.pattern: lots of [determiner + noun] · lots of [object pronoun] · [verb] lots (We have lots) · there are lots left · lots more
entries.contrast: Lots is a lot with the volume turned up and the register turned down; both beat much and many in positive statements, and both are out of place in formal prose, where the choices are many, much, a great deal, and a large number. Unlike a lot, lots is awkward as a bare subject — Lots were left over is possible but strained, and There were lots left over is what people say.
entries.see also: a lot, a great deal, many, much, plenty, several, lots of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large number of countable things, presented as large.
examples: Many of the houses on that street have been rebuilt.
Not many showed up for the second meeting.
How many of them are still under warranty?
She has written a dozen books, and many are still in print.
Of the applicants we interviewed, many had no experience at all.
Many were called, but few were chosen.
entries.pronunciation note: note the /ɛ/, not /æ/: it does not rhyme with Annie
entries.русский: многие, много — только о счётных; для неисчисляемого — much
entries.register: neutral; bare many as a subject is somewhat formal
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, many books, and the archaic many a + singular noun)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a large number of countable things or people. Never a mass — ✗many of the water; for a mass the word is much.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Many were called; Many of the houses were damaged. There is no singular use of the pronoun. (The singular many a man was lost is a determiner construction and a separate, archaic pattern.)
entries.pattern: many [plural verb] · many of [determiner + plural noun] · many of [object pronoun] · [verb] many (I don't have many) · how many, not many, too many, so many, as many, a good many · many more, many others
entries.the register point: in a positive statement bare many sounds formal (Many disagree), and ordinary speech uses a lot or lots; in negatives, in questions, and after too, so, as, and how, many is completely natural (Not many showed up, How many are left?). Against few: many is a large number, few a small number with a negative slant, several a middling handful.
entries.contrast: Many vs. much — many counts, much measures: many mistakes, much confusion.
entries.see also: much, few, a few, several, more, most, a lot, many (determiner)

entries.meaning: A greater amount or number than what came before, or than what was expected.
examples: There's coffee in the pot if you want more.
More of the guests are staying over than we planned for.
We expected fifty and got more.
Half the roof is gone, and more is coming down every week.
She said little, but more was implied than stated.
Of the twenty crates, more were damaged than intact.
entries.pronunciation note: keeps its vowel unstressed; more of them runs together as /ˈmɔrəvəm/ · MOR-uh-vum
entries.русский: больше, ещё — большее количество или число, чем некий ориентир
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: comparative quantifying pronoun — the comparative of both much and many (also a determiner, more chairs, and the adverb of comparison, more slowly)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: a greater amount of a mass or a greater number of countables than some stated or implied benchmark. Things, people, or abstractions.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — More of the roof is gone than we thought (mass → singular); More of the guests are staying over (countable → plural). Bare More is needed is singular; More were expected is plural. Because more serves as the comparative of much and of many at once, the word itself carries no number.
entries.pattern: more [verb] · more of [determiner + noun] · more of [object pronoun] · [verb] more · more than [amount / noun phrase] · no more, some more, any more, many more, much more, one more, a lot more
entries.contrast: More is the comparative of both much and many, which is exactly why it takes either number — the choice is made by the referent, not by the word. Its opposites, however, do split by type: fewer for countables, less for a mass. Against another: another is one additional single item (I'll have another), more an additional quantity (I'll have more). Against most: more compares two, most tops the whole set.
entries.see also: most, less, fewer, much, many, another, more (determiner)

entries.meaning: The majority of a group, or the greater part of a quantity.
examples: Most of the paint had already peeled off.
Most of them had never used the software before.
She kept most and sold the rest.
Most agree that the deadline is unrealistic.
Of the six proposals, most were rejected on the first pass.
He does the least talking and gets the most done.
entries.pronunciation note: in casual speech the final cluster reduces before a consonant: most people /ˈmoʊs ˈpipl̩/
entries.русский: большинство, бо́льшая часть — и о счётных, и о массе
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: superlative quantifying pronoun — the superlative of both much and many (also a determiner, most people, and the degree adverb, most likely)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: the greater part of a mass or the majority of a set of countables. Things or people. Bare most as a subject generalizes about people (Most agree that…).
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — Most of the cake was eaten (mass → singular); Most of the students were absent (countable → plural); Most agree (people → plural).
entries.pattern: most [verb] · most of [determiner + noun] · most of [object pronoun] · [verb] most · the most (superlative over a definite comparison: whoever sells the most) · at most, for the most part (adverbial idioms)
entries.contrast: Most vs. most of. Before a specific set the of is required — most of the students means these particular ones, while the determiner most students is a generalization about students at large. Before a pronoun the of is not optional: most of them, ✗most them. Most vs. the most: most is a majority; the most is the largest amount in an explicit comparison (Whoever sells the most wins). Like more, most is the superlative of both much and many, which is why it takes either number.
entries.see also: more, all, many, much, some, least, most (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large amount of something measured rather than counted.
examples: There isn't much left in the account.
Much of what he said was guesswork.
How much did you end up paying?
Much has been written about the case, most of it wrong.
She didn't say much about the interview.
We have too much of it as it is.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form
entries.русский: много (неисчисляемого) — нейтрально в отрицаниях и вопросах, в утверждениях натянуто
entries.register: neutral in negatives and questions; stilted in plain positive statements
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, much time, and an adverb of degree, much better, thanks so much)
entries.person / number: third person; always singular
entries.refers to: a large amount of a mass or an abstraction — never countable things. For countables the word is many.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Much of the report is redundant; Much has been written about it. There is no plural use; and since it cannot take a plural of-phrase in the first place (✗much of the people), no plural attraction can arise.
entries.pattern: much [singular verb] · much of [determiner + mass noun] · much of [it / this / that] · [verb] much (I don't have much) · how much, not much, too much, so much, as much, very much, nothing much · much of a [noun] (not much of a plan)
entries.the register trap that matters more: in an ordinary positive statement bare much is not idiomatic American English — ✗I ate much, ✗We have much — and the natural word is a lot. Reserve much for negatives (I didn't eat much), questions (How much is left?), the too / so / as / how frames, and a handful of fixed formal phrases where it survives in the affirmative: much has changed, much remains to be done, so much the better.
entries.contrast: Much vs. many — mass versus count, and the division is absolute.
entries.see also: many, little, a little, more, most, a lot, a great deal, less, much (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large quantity, said cheerfully.
examples: She has oodles of time and no idea what to do with it.
There's oodles left in the freezer.
Oodles of them were handed out along the parade route.
He inherited the house and oodles besides.
Oodles of the frosting ended up on the floor.
We asked for a little help and got oodles.
entries.pronunciation note: the second syllable is a syllabic /l/ with no vowel of its own
entries.русский: уйма, целая куча — разг.-шутл., амер., слегка старомодно
entries.register: informal and playful — American colloquial, mid-nineteenth-century in origin and now faintly old-fashioned; the word people use with children or for comic effect, and never in formal prose
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, oodles of money)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large amount of a mass or number of countables, named with obvious cheer — money, time, room, attention. There is no singular: ✗an oodle.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent — Oodles of them were given away (countable → plural); Oodles of money was spent (mass → singular).
entries.pattern: oodles of [determiner + noun] · oodles of [object pronoun] · [verb] oodles (We have oodles) · oodles more · the fixed oodles of noodles
entries.contrast: Against lots, loads, and tons: all four are informal words for a large quantity, and oodles is the only one that is also jocular — using it is a small stylistic act, and readers hear the whimsy whether or not it was intended. Against scads, gobs, and a slew: the same American family of hyperbolic quantity words, none of which belongs in edited prose. Bare oodles as a subject is rare; the word wants an of-phrase or an object slot.
entries.see also: lots, loads, tons, a ton, heaps, a lot, plenty, oodles of (determiner)

entries.ipa: /ˈplɛnti/, with the American dropped /t/ after /n/ also /ˈplɛni/
entries.meaning: More than enough of something — a comfortable sufficiency.
examples: Don't bring chairs — we have plenty.
Plenty of them had already heard the news.
There's plenty left if you're still hungry.
She had plenty to say once the meeting ended.
Plenty of the equipment was still under warranty.
Of the free tickets, plenty went unclaimed.
entries.русский: полно, вдоволь — вполне достаточно, и о счётных, и о массе
entries.register: neutral to informal
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, plenty of room, and an informal adverb, plenty big)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: an amply sufficient amount of a mass or number of countables — things, people, time, money. It covers both types, which is part of why speakers reach for it instead of choosing between much and many.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — Plenty of the seats are still open (countable → plural); Plenty of time remains (mass → singular). There's plenty is singular on a mass reading; There are plenty left is plural when the referent is countable.
entries.pattern: plenty [verb] · plenty of [determiner + noun] · plenty of [object pronoun] · [verb] plenty (We have plenty) · there's plenty · plenty more, plenty else
entries.contrast: Against enough: enough is the amount needed and no more; plenty is comfortably beyond it — We have enough settles the question, We have plenty closes it. Against much and many: plenty is type-neutral and does not force the count/mass choice. Note that plenty of takes no article (✗a plenty of chairs), and that the noun a plenty is archaic. The Southern and Appalachian aplenty (food aplenty) is a regional postposed adverb, not this pronoun, and should be labeled as such.
entries.see also: enough, a lot, lots, a great deal, much, many, plenty of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A fairly large number — the idiom whose parts point the wrong way.
examples: Quite a few of the seats were still open at showtime.
She asked for volunteers and got quite a few.
Quite a few of them had done this kind of work before.
Of the sixty who registered, quite a few never showed up.
He has written quite a few on the subject and been wrong about most of it.
There were complaints, quite a few, and not one of them was answered.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and the /t/ of quite is normally a flap in front of it, kwy-duh-FYOO
entries.русский: немало, порядочно — о счётных, больше, чем ожидает собеседник
entries.register: neutral to informal — ordinary in speech and in any writing that is not stiff
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — a few with quite in front of it, and not a small quantity in spite of its parts (also a determiner, quite a few years)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a fairly large number of countable things or people, presented as more than the listener would expect. Never a mass: ✗quite a few of the water; the mass counterpart is quite a bit.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Quite a few were damaged; Quite a few of the seats are still open.
entries.pattern: quite a few [plural verb] · quite a few of [determiner + plural noun] · quite a few of [object pronoun] · [verb] quite a few · the determiner quite a few + plural noun (quite a few years) · the mass twin quite a bit
entries.contrast: The idiom reverses its own parts. A few is a small number and quite is an intensifier, so the phrase ought to mean "a very small number," and it means the opposite — a fairly large one. Quite a bit does the same thing for a mass, while quite a lot means exactly what it looks like, which is what makes the pair a reliable trap for learners. Against a good many: the same quantity a notch more formal. Against several: smaller, and neutral about expectation. Against bare few: the opposite sign entirely — few of them came is a complaint that almost nobody did, quite a few of them came is a report that a lot did, and two words separate them.
entries.see also: a few, few, a good many, several, many, a lot, a bit, quite a few (determiner), quite a bit of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A large quantity, in a casual American plural with no singular behind it.
examples: There were scads of them for sale at the flea market.
She has scads of relatives in the county and sees none of them.
Scads of the tickets went unsold.
He made scads on the patent and lost it all on the next one.
There's scads left if anybody is still hungry.
We expected a dozen replies and got scads.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; one syllable, and there is no singular — ✗a scad is not a word in this sense
entries.русский: уйма, куча — амер. разг., слегка старомодно
entries.register: informal and American — mid-nineteenth-century in origin, casual and a little old-fashioned now; not for formal prose
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, scads of money)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass — people, tickets, relatives, money, time. Plural in form only, and with no singular of any kind behind it.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent, not with the -s — Scads of them were printed (countable → plural); Scads of money was poured into it (mass → singular).
entries.pattern: scads of [determiner + noun] · scads of [object pronoun] · [verb] scads (We have scads) · there are scads left · scads more
entries.contrast: Against gobs: the nearest relative, and the two are interchangeable in practice. Against oodles: playful where scads is merely casual. Against tons, loads, and lots: the unmarked informal words, and the ones nobody notices. Bare scads as a subject is awkward — Scads were left over is possible and strained, and There were scads left over is what people actually say. And note that the word has no singular at all, which is what separates it from a bunch, a ton, and a boatload.
entries.see also: gobs, oodles, tons, loads, heaps, lots, a slew, scores of (determiner), oodles of (determiner)

entries.meaning: An indefinite but more than token number of things — a handful, but a decent one.
examples: Several of the panels had come loose.
She called all morning, and several of the calls went straight to voicemail.
I only needed one, but I bought several.
Several were still waiting when the office closed.
Of the applicants, several had worked there before.
He made several of the same mistakes again.
entries.pronunciation note: the middle vowel normally drops, leaving two syllables
entries.русский: несколько — больше двух-трёх, но меньше, чем many; только о счётных
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun (also a determiner, several people)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: an indefinite number of countable things or people — more than two or three, fewer than many. Never a mass: ✗several of the water, ✗several of the furniture.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Several were damaged in transit; Several of the windows are cracked.
entries.pattern: several [plural verb] · several of [determiner + plural noun] · several of [object pronoun] · [verb] several (I bought several) · several more, several others
entries.contrast: Several sits between a few and many — more than a few, fewer than many — and unlike few it carries no complaint in it. It is strictly countable, so the mass equivalents are some and a little. Watch the false friend: in legal English several means "separate, individual" (joint and several liability, the several states), an adjective with nothing to do with quantity.
entries.see also: a few, a couple, few, many, some, others, several (determiner)

entries.meaning: The plural of the American exaggeration, and the commoner of its two shapes. ---
examples: Don't bring food — we have tons.
Tons of them were still sitting unopened in the garage.
There's tons left if you want more.
She has read tons about the case and still can't explain it.
Tons of the wiring had to be replaced.
I expected a handful of replies and got tons.
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; the vowel is the one in sun
entries.русский: куча, море — обычное амер. разг. преувеличение
entries.register: informal — the ordinary American exaggeration in speech and casual writing
entries.type: hyperbolic quantifying pronoun (also a quantifier before of + noun, tons of work, an informal adverb, tons better, and the plural of the unit of weight)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, in spite of the -s
entries.refers to: a large number of countables or a large amount of a mass — things, people, time, money, work.
entries.agreement: agrees with the referent, not with the -s — Tons of people were there (countable → plural); Tons of the paint was wasted (mass → singular). The literal weights keep a real plural, and there the -s does count: Three tons of gravel were delivered.
entries.pattern: tons of [determiner + noun] · tons of [object pronoun] · [verb] tons (We have tons) · there are tons left · tons more · adverbial tons better, and the fixed singular thanks a ton
entries.contrast: Against a ton: one word, one agreement rule, two shapes — the plural is the commoner before of, and the singular is what survives in thanks a ton and it helped a ton. Against lots and loads: interchangeable in register and meaning, with tons the most plainly American of the three. Against the unit of weight: only the context tells you whether anything was weighed, and if the number matters, write two tons and be done with it. In formal writing, many, much, or a great deal.
entries.see also: a ton, lots, loads, heaps, oodles, a lot, a bunch, tons of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small amount of something measured, offered as some rather than none.
examples: There's a bit left in the bottom of the pot.
A bit of the plaster had come away above the window.
She knows a bit about wiring, enough to be dangerous.
He saved a bit every month for eleven years.
I've heard a bit of it, but not the whole story.
Quite a bit of the money never reached the school.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and never stressed; the final /t/ is usually unreleased or glottal at the end of a phrase, and flapped before a vowel — a bit of it /əˈbɪdəvɪt/
entries.русский: немного, чуть-чуть — о неисчисляемом; мало, но всё же есть
entries.register: neutral to informal — the everyday small-quantity word in speech
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a bit of luck, an adverb of degree, a bit tired, and an ordinary count noun, a bit of string)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: a small but positive amount of a mass or an abstraction — time, money, luck, trouble, information. Never countables: ✗a bit of the chairs; for a small number the phrase is a few.
entries.agreement: singular, always — A bit of it is left; A bit of the plaster has come away.
entries.pattern: a bit [singular verb] · a bit of [determiner + mass noun] · a bit of [it / this / that] · [verb] a bit (I ate a bit) · a bit more, a bit less, quite a bit, every bit · adverbial a bit late, wait a bit, a bit of a mess
entries.contrast: Against a little: the two are all but identical in the pronoun slot and differ only in tone, a bit being the more casual — There's a little left and There's a bit left say the same thing. The idiom to watch is quite a bit, which means a fairly large amount — the same reversal that turns a few into quite a few. Against a little bit: a common and unobjectionable doubling, one degree more informal again. And note that most of this word's daily work is adverbial (a bit tired, a bit of a mess), where it modifies something rather than standing in for it.
entries.see also: a little, little, a few, a handful, less, some, a bit of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small number of countable things, normally two and loosely two or three.
examples: There were sandwiches left, so I took a couple.
A couple of them had already gone home.
She asked for volunteers and got a couple.
A couple of the panels were loose.
I gave a copy to a couple of the neighbors.
Of the twelve applicants, only a couple had the certification.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and never stressed; before of the whole phrase runs together, a couple of them /əˈkʌpləvəm/ · uh-KUP-luh-vum
entries.русский: пара, парочка — строго двое, в разг. речи двое-трое
entries.register: informal to neutral; in formal writing two or a few is the safer choice
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a couple of days, and an ordinary count noun, a married couple)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a small number of countable things or people — strictly two, and loosely two or three. Never a mass: ✗a couple of the water.
entries.agreement: plural, always — A couple were left over; A couple of the panels are loose. (The count noun a couple meaning a pair of people takes either number depending on whether they are seen as a unit or as two individuals — The couple was married in June, The couple were arguing — but the quantifying pronoun is invariably plural.)
entries.pattern: a couple [plural verb] · a couple of [determiner + plural noun] · a couple of [object pronoun] · [verb] a couple (I'll take a couple) · a couple more, a couple others
entries.contrast: Against two: two is exact, a couple is approximate in ordinary American use, and a couple of days frequently means three. Against a few: a few is vaguer and runs higher; the two overlap and either is usually fine. The of is not optional in edited writing: before a pronoun it is required outright (a couple of them, ✗a couple them), and a couple of days is the edited form of the very common spoken ✗a couple days — widespread informal American usage that copy editors still change. Keep the pronoun apart from the count noun in the couple next door, which takes an ordinary plural (two couples).
entries.see also: a few, few, several, some, ones, a couple of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small number of countable things, offered as enough to matter.
examples: A few of the parts were missing from the box.
I know a few who would take that job tomorrow.
There were sandwiches left, so I took a few.
A few of us stayed behind to clean up.
Quite a few of the seats were still available at showtime.
He asked for volunteers and got a few.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always reduced to /ə/ and never stressed
entries.русский: несколько — мало, но всё же есть; ср. few «мало, недостаточно»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a determiner, a few people)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a small but positive number of countable things or people — "some, and that counts for something." Never a mass; for a small amount of a mass the phrase is a little.
entries.agreement: plural, always — A few were left over; A few of the guests are still here.
entries.pattern: a few [plural verb] · a few of [determiner + plural noun] · a few of [object pronoun] · [verb] a few · quite a few · a few more, a few others
entries.the idiom to watch: quite a few means a fairly large number, the opposite of what its parts suggest. Against several: several is a bit more, but the two overlap and either is usually fine.
entries.contrast: A few vs. few — the article changes the sign. A few of the guests stayed means some stayed, and that is reported as a positive fact; Few of the guests stayed means almost nobody did, and it is a complaint. The same flip runs through a little and little.
entries.see also: few, a couple, a little, several, some, fewer, a few (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small number of countable things, named as smaller than expected.
examples: Only a handful of the invitations came back.
A handful of us stayed to finish the count.
She expected a crowd and got a handful.
A handful of them had done the reading.
Of the sixty applicants, a handful had any experience at all.
He named a handful of the people involved and stopped there.
entries.pronunciation note: the /d/ normally drops between the /n/ and the /f/, uh-HAN-fool; the article is always reduced to /ə/
entries.русский: горстка, считаные единицы — небольшое число счётных, меньше ожидаемого
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a quantifier before of + noun, a handful of people, an ordinary count noun, a handful of sand, and an informal predicate noun, that child is a handful)
entries.person / number: third person; plural in the quantifying use
entries.refers to: a small number of countable things or people — five or six, loosely, and always presented as fewer than there might have been. Never a mass; for a small amount the words are a little and a bit.
entries.agreement: plural in the quantifying use — A handful of them were still waiting; Only a handful have replied. The literal count noun is singular: A handful of sand was all that came up. The split is the same one that separates a couple the quantifier from a couple the pair of people.
entries.pattern: a handful [plural verb] · a handful of [determiner + plural noun] · a handful of [object pronoun] · [verb] a handful · only a handful, no more than a handful, a mere handful
entries.contrast: Against a few and several: a few is neutral about the count, several runs a little higher, and a handful is the one that says openly that the number is small and probably disappointing — it is few with a friendlier face. Against a couple: two or three against five or six. Keep the quantifier apart from the two nouns it grew out of — the literal fistful (a handful of gravel) and the person who is hard work (He's a handful) — neither of which is this pronoun.
entries.see also: a few, a couple, several, few, some, a bit, a handful of (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small amount of something measured, presented as some rather than none.
examples: There's still a little left in the bottle.
A little of the mortar had crumbled away.
She speaks Portuguese — not fluently, but a little.
A little goes a long way with that spice.
He knew a little about engines and nothing about wiring.
I've saved a little of the money for later.
entries.pronunciation note: with the American flapped or glottalized /t/, closer to uh-LIH-dul
entries.русский: немного — о неисчисляемом: мало, но есть; ср. little «мало, недостаточно»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase (also a determiner, a little milk, and an adverb of degree, a little tired)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: a small but positive amount of a mass or abstraction. Never countables — ✗a little of the cookies; for a small number the phrase is a few.
entries.agreement: singular, always — A little of the paint is left; A little goes a long way.
entries.pattern: a little [singular verb] · a little of [determiner + mass noun] · a little of [it / this / that] · [verb] a little (I ate a little) · a little more, a little less
entries.contrast: A little vs. little — the article flips the sign exactly as it does with a few and few: There's a little left is reassuring, There's little left is a warning. A little vs. a few — mass versus count. And note that in a little tired or wait a little the phrase is an adverb of degree or duration, not this pronoun.
entries.see also: little, a few, less, much, some, a little (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small number, presented as smaller than it should be.
examples: Few of the original members are still on the board.
Many applied; few were hired.
Few of us had ever seen anything like it.
Of the promises made that spring, few survived the summer.
Few have read the report all the way through.
The few who stayed did most of the work.
entries.русский: мало, немногие — с оттенком «недостаточно»; ср. a few «несколько»
entries.register: neutral in writing; formal-sounding in speech, where not many is the usual substitute
entries.type: quantifying pronoun, negative in force (also a determiner, few people)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a small number of countable things or people, presented as insufficient or disappointing. Never a mass; the mass counterpart is little.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Few were willing to say so publicly; Few of the changes have been implemented.
entries.pattern: few [plural verb] · few of [determiner + plural noun] · few of [object pronoun] · the few (the few who stayed) · very few, so few, too few, how few · comparative fewer, superlative fewest
entries.contrast: Few vs. a few — dropping the article makes the word negative: Few of them came is a complaint; A few of them came is not. Few vs. little — count versus mass. Few vs. the few — the few names a specific small group (the few who bothered to vote) rather than reporting a shortage. In everyday speech, bare few as a subject sounds bookish; people say not many or hardly any.
entries.see also: a few, a couple, fewer, fewest, little, many, several, none, few (determiner)

entries.meaning: A smaller number of countable things than before, or than something else.
examples: Fewer of the students showed up than last semester.
There were forty complaints last quarter and fewer this one.
Fewer than half of them were returned.
Of the twelve original tenants, fewer remain each year.
She made mistakes, but fewer than anyone expected.
Fewer are willing to work weekends now.
entries.русский: меньше по числу — только о счётных; для неисчисляемого — less
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: comparative quantifying pronoun — the comparative of few (also a determiner, fewer mistakes)
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: a smaller number of countable things or people than some benchmark. Never a mass — that is less.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Fewer of the seats were occupied this year; Fewer are applying than a decade ago.
entries.pattern: fewer [plural verb] · fewer of [determiner + plural noun] · fewer of [object pronoun] · [verb] fewer · fewer than [number] · far fewer, no fewer than, the fewest
entries.contrast: Fewer vs. less — stated honestly. The rule taught in school is count with fewer, measure with less: fewer bottles, less water; in pronoun position, Fewer of the bottles were returned but Less of the water was wasted. The rule holds well in edited American prose and a conservative editor will enforce it, but it is a usage convention, not a law of the language — less has been used with countables since Old English, and it is fully standard before amounts treated as a single measure: less than three miles, less than fifty dollars, less than two weeks, where ✗fewer than two weeks is actually wrong. The supermarket sign 10 items or less is idiomatic English that editors dislike. Practical rule: when the referent is a plural count noun, fewer is always safe.
entries.see also: fewest, less, few, more, least, many, fewer (determiner)

entries.meaning: The smallest number of countable things in a comparison.
examples: Of the four teams, ours had the fewest.
She made the fewest of anyone in the class.
The fewest were sold in the week after the recall.
He compared the three routes and took the one with the fewest.
Whoever files the fewest still has to file something.
Among the three branches, the downtown office reported the fewest.
entries.pronunciation note: three sounds in the second syllable, not two; ✗FYOOST is a reduction that reads as a mistake in careful speech
entries.русский: меньше всего по числу — превосх. от few, о счётных; для массы — least
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: superlative quantifying pronoun, almost always with the — the superlative of few (also a determiner, the fewest mistakes)
entries.person / number: third person; plural
entries.refers to: the smallest number of countable things or people, in a comparison across three or more. Never a mass — the mass superlative is least.
entries.agreement: plural — The fewest were sold in the week after the recall. When the fewest is the object, the verb belongs to some other subject and takes that subject's number: Whichever branch reports the fewest gets the bonus.
entries.pattern: the fewest [plural verb] · the fewest of [determiner + plural noun] · [verb] the fewest (she made the fewest) · the fewest possible · the second fewest, by far the fewest
entries.contrast: Fewest is to few what least is to little — count against mass — and it completes the few / fewer / fewest series that the file's fewer entry sets up. With exactly two the word is fewer, not fewest: the fewer of the two. In practice fewest is much commoner as a determiner (the fewest mistakes) than as a bare pronoun, and speakers routinely reach for least where the referent is countable — the least mistakes is ordinary in speech and is exactly what a copy editor changes to the fewest mistakes. The same honesty applies here as under fewer: the count/measure split is a well-entrenched editing convention rather than a law of the language, but with a plural count referent fewest is always the safe choice.
entries.see also: few, fewer, least, less, most, fewest (determiner)

entries.meaning: The smallest amount, or the thing that matters or counts for the smallest amount.
examples: The cost is the least of our problems right now.
He does the least and complains the most.
Buying dinner was the least I could do.
Whoever contributes the least still gets an equal share.
The least of the three estimates still came to nine thousand dollars.
That was the least of what he told the investigators.
entries.русский: меньше всего, наименьшее количество — о неисчисляемом или по рангу
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: superlative quantifying pronoun, almost always with the — the superlative of little and less (also a determiner, the least trouble, and a degree adverb, least likely)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: the smallest amount of a mass or abstraction, or the lowest-ranking item in a comparison. Not normally used for a number of countables — the count superlative is fewest.
entries.agreement: singular — The least of my worries is the paperwork; Least said, soonest mended.
entries.pattern: the least of [noun phrase] · [verb] the least · the least [subject] could do · at least, not in the least, least of all, last but not least (fixed adverbial idioms, a different word class)
entries.contrast: Least is to little what fewest is to few — mass against count. Most of the word's daily life is spent inside fixed phrases where it is no longer a pronoun at all: at least and not in the least are adverbials. As a genuine pronoun it appears mainly in the least of + noun phrase (the least of our problems) and in comparisons of amount (he does the least).
entries.see also: less, little, fewer, fewest, most, least (determiner)

entries.meaning: A smaller amount of something measured, or a lower degree of something.
examples: There's less of it left than I thought.
Less was recovered from the second site than from the first.
She wanted more responsibility and got less.
Less of the budget went to maintenance this year.
It costs less than the model we looked at first.
Traffic is less of a problem on this side of town.
entries.русский: меньше по количеству — о неисчисляемом, а также о мерах: less than three miles
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: comparative quantifying pronoun — the comparative of little (also a determiner, less noise, an adverb of degree, less often, and a marginal preposition of subtraction, five less two)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: a smaller amount of a mass or abstraction; also, in fully standard idiom, a smaller measured amount even when the noun behind it is countable — less than three miles, less than two weeks.
entries.agreement: singular — Less of the money was recovered than expected; Less is known about the second case.
entries.pattern: less [singular verb] · less of [determiner + mass noun] · less of [it / this / that] · [verb] less · less than [amount] · much less, no less, nothing less, far less · less of a [noun] (less of a problem)
entries.contrast: Less vs. fewer — the full account is under fewer; the short version is that countable things take fewer and measured amounts take less, with money, distance, weight, and time going to less even though their nouns are plural. Less also owns a construction fewer cannot enter at all: less of a problem, less of a hassle, where the noun is singular and the sense is degree rather than number. Do not confuse less with the adjective lesser (the lesser of two evils), which grades importance, not quantity.
entries.see also: fewer, little, a little, least, more, much, less (determiner)

entries.meaning: A small amount of something, presented as too small. ---
examples: Little is known about what happened after midnight.
He said little and left early.
Little of the original wiring is still in place.
She gave a great deal and asked for little.
Too little was done, and far too late.
Of the money raised that year, little ever reached the school.
entries.pronunciation note: with the American flap, LIH-dul
entries.русский: мало — о неисчисляемом, с оттенком «недостаточно»; ср. a little «немного»
entries.register: neutral in writing; formal-sounding in speech, where not much is the usual substitute
entries.type: quantifying pronoun, negative in force (also a determiner, little time, an adjective of size, a little dog, and a fronting adverb, little did he know)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: a small amount of a mass or abstraction, presented as insufficient — the mass counterpart of few. Never countables.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Little is known about him; Little of the original building remains.
entries.pattern: little [singular verb] · little of [determiner + mass noun] · little of [it / this / that] · [verb] little (He said little) · very little, so little, too little, precious little · comparative less, superlative least
entries.contrast: Little vs. a little — the article flips the sign: little is hardly any and is a complaint; a little is some and is not. Little vs. few — mass against count. And keep this pronoun apart from the adjective little meaning small (a little house, my little brother), which is a different word entirely and has nothing to do with quantity — the giveaway is that the adjective sits in front of a noun and can be graded (littler, littlest), while the pronoun stands alone.
entries.see also: a little, less, least, few, much, little (determiner)

entries.meaning: The part of an amount that is still outstanding.
examples: A deposit is due at signing and the balance on delivery.
He paid half in March and the balance the following spring.
The balance of the estate went to her nephew.
She served two years of the contract and forfeited the balance.
The insurer covered the first ten thousand dollars and the family paid the balance.
The balance of the term will be taught by a substitute.
entries.pronunciation note: the is the weak /ðə/ here, as it is before any consonant
entries.русский: остаток, сальдо — фин. и коммерч., чаще о недоплаченной сумме
entries.register: formal and commercial — accounting, contracts, invoices, and business letters; the plain-English word is the rest
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the noun balance used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, the balance of the term)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular with a sum or a mass and plural with countables
entries.refers to: what is left of a quantity after part of it has been paid, taken, delivered, or used — most often a sum of money still owed, and by extension any remainder at all.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — The balance is due on the first (a sum, singular, and by far the commonest case); The balance of the crates were damaged in transit (countables, plural). The word attaches to amounts far more readily than to countable things, so the singular dominates.
entries.pattern: the balance [verb] · the balance of [determiner + noun] · [verb] the balance · the balance due, pay the balance, the balance of the term, the balance of the evidence
entries.contrast: Against the rest and the remainder: the three name the same leftover in three registers — the rest is the plain word, the remainder the formal one, and the balance the commercial one, which keeps a faint suggestion of an account to be settled even where no money is involved (the balance of the season). Against the ordinary noun balance meaning equilibrium (he lost his balance) or the weighing instrument: the same spelling and an unrelated sense.
entries.see also: the rest, the remainder, the majority, others, more, the rest of, the remainder of (determiner)

entries.meaning: More than half of a group, taken as a quantity.
examples: The majority of the tenants signed the petition.
Of the six proposals, the majority were sent back for revision.
She won a second term, but the majority was down to eleven votes.
The majority of them had never voted in a primary before.
The vast majority of the complaints concerned noise.
The majority were willing to wait; a loud few were not.
entries.pronunciation note: the medial /t/ is normally a flap in American speech, muh-JOR-uh-dee
entries.русский: большинство — только о счётных; о деньгах и массе — most, не the majority
entries.register: neutral to formal — the word of journalism, reports, and minutes; most is the everyday equivalent
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the noun majority used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, the majority of voters, and an ordinary count noun, a two-thirds majority)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with the members and singular with the bloc or the margin
entries.refers to: more than half of a set of countable people or things. Never a mass: most of the money is right and ✗the majority of the money is not, and that count/mass line is the sharpest practical difference between this phrase and most.
entries.agreement: plural with the members, singular with the bloc. The majority of the residents were opposed (the people, and this is the ordinary case); The majority was slim (the margin); A working majority has controlled the chamber since (the group as one thing). American editors accept both and choose by sense.
entries.pattern: the majority [verb] · the majority of [determiner + plural noun] · the majority of [object pronoun] · the vast majority, the overwhelming majority, the bare majority · in the majority, by a majority of [number]
entries.contrast: Majority vs. most. Most covers mass and count alike and belongs in every register; the majority takes countables only and sounds official, which is why most of the money is right and the bureaucratic ✗the majority of the money is wrong. Where the members can be counted, either word works: most of the voters, the majority of the voters. Against the minority: the two halves of one division. Against a plurality: a plurality is the largest share without being more than half — the winner of a three-way race with forty percent has a plurality and not a majority, and the difference matters in reporting an election.
entries.see also: the minority, most, more, all, the rest, some, the majority of, the minority of (determiner), a plurality of (determiner)

entries.meaning: Fewer than half of a group, taken as a quantity.
examples: The minority on the committee filed a separate report.
The minority were never asked what they wanted.
She was in the minority on that vote and said so afterward.
Of the twelve jurors, the minority held out for three days.
In the minority of cases where the drug fails, the symptoms return within a week.
The majority wanted to wait; the minority wanted to sue.
entries.pronunciation note: the medial /t/ is normally a flap, my-NOR-uh-dee
entries.русский: меньшинство — менее половины счётного множества
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the noun minority used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, and a count noun with several unrelated senses)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with the members and singular with the bloc or the share
entries.refers to: fewer than half of a set of countable people or things. Never a mass: for a small amount the words are less and a little.
entries.agreement: plural with the members, singular with the bloc — The minority were never consulted (the people); The minority was vocal but small (the group as one thing). Both are standard and the sense decides, exactly as with the majority.
entries.pattern: the minority [verb] · the minority of [determiner + plural noun] · the minority of [object pronoun] · a small minority, a vocal minority, a tiny minority · in the minority · in the minority of cases
entries.contrast: Against the majority: the two halves of the same division, and both are countable-only. Against few and a few: those report a small number without reference to any whole, while the minority is explicitly the smaller part of a set that has been divided. The other sense of the word. In American English minority far more often names an ethnic or racial group that is not the dominant one — minority students, minority-owned businesses — and that is a noun and a modifier rather than this pronoun. Because the two senses share a spelling, a sentence like the minority were unhappy can be read either way; naming the group, or writing the smaller group, removes the ambiguity.
entries.see also: the majority, few, a few, less, least, some, the majority of, the minority of (determiner)

entries.meaning: What is left after part has been taken, said formally.
examples: The remainder of the shipment arrived on Thursday.
He read the first two chapters carefully and skimmed the remainder.
The remainder of the money was returned to the donors.
She will teach the class for the remainder of the term.
Two of the panels were salvageable; the remainder had to be scrapped.
Of the original grant, the remainder is barely enough for one more season.
entries.pronunciation note: the first vowel of remainder is a reduced /ɪ/ or /ə/ and never carries stress
entries.русский: остаток, оставшаяся часть — книжн. и офиц.; в обиходе the rest
entries.register: formal — reports, contracts, and technical prose; in ordinary writing the phrase is the rest
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the noun remainder used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, and a technical noun in arithmetic and in bookselling)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass
entries.refers to: what is left of a set or a quantity after part of it has been removed, used, or accounted for — things, people, time, or an amount.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — The remainder of the crates were shipped Tuesday (countable → plural); The remainder of the money was returned (mass → singular). Bare The remainder is yours is singular on an amount reading and The remainder are unaccounted for plural on a count reading.
entries.pattern: the remainder [verb] · the remainder of [determiner + noun] · the remainder of [object pronoun] · [verb] the remainder · for the remainder of the year
entries.contrast: Against the rest: the same meaning a register up, and the rest is what a plain-English editor substitutes nine times out of ten. Against the balance: the commercial version, tied to sums owed. Against others and the others: those are countable and usually personal — the others left is people, the remainder was discarded is stuff. Two technical senses are not this pronoun at all: the remainder left over from a division in arithmetic, and remainders, the unsold books a publisher clears at a discount.
entries.see also: the rest, the balance, the majority, others, other, more, the rest of, the remainder of (determiner)

entries.meaning: What is left of an estate after everything else has been paid out — the fused head of a will.
examples: The residue passes to the testator's sister in equal shares with her children.
After the specific bequests were satisfied, the residue came to less than anyone expected.
The will was drafted without a residuary clause, so the residue fell into intestacy.
She left the house to her nephew and the residue to a scholarship fund.
Debts and taxes are paid first, and the residue is divided only after that.
The old form gave "the rest, residue and remainder" where the residue alone would have done.
entries.pronunciation note: American English drops the yod, so it is REZ-uh-doo and not the British REZ-i-dyoo; the is the weak /ðə/ before the consonant
entries.русский: юр.: остаток наследства после долгов, налогов и завещательных отказов
entries.register: formal and legal — the language of wills, trusts, and probate above all. An American meets it in a will, in a probate filing, or in a letter from an estate lawyer, and essentially nowhere else.
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the noun residue used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, the residue of the estate, and an ordinary noun in chemistry and cooking)
entries.person / number: third person; singular in the legal use, where it names an estate; elsewhere it takes its number from the referent
entries.refers to: what is left of an estate after debts, taxes, expenses, and specific gifts have been paid out — the technical sense behind residuary estate, residuary clause, and residuary legatee. By extension, and much more rarely, whatever is left of anything at all.
entries.agreement: singular in the legal sense — The residue passes to the testator's sister; The residue of the estate is to be divided equally. On the rare general use it agrees with what it refers to, exactly as the remainder does.
entries.pattern: the residue [singular verb] · the residue of [determiner + noun] · [verb] the residue · I give the residue to [beneficiary] · the residuary estate, the residuary clause, the residuary legatee (the adjective, not this pronoun)
entries.contrast: Against the remainder: the ordinary formal word for the same idea, usable in any kind of writing, where the residue is narrow and outside a will sounds either technical or faintly chemical. Against the rest: the plain-English word, and the one a modern drafter now writes even in a will — the classic legal triplet the rest, residue and remainder of my estate is three words doing one word's work, and plain-language drafting guides cut it to the rest. Against the balance: the commercial version, tied to sums owed. And keep the pronoun apart from the everyday noun residue meaning a film or a deposit (soap residue, pesticide residue), which is far the commoner sense of the word.
entries.see also: the remainder, the rest, the balance, the whole, others, the premises, the undersigned, the rest of, the remainder of (determiner)

entries.meaning: Everything or everyone that is left. ---
examples: She ate two slices and left the rest.
The rest of them were still out in the parking lot.
The rest of the paint had dried solid in the can.
He spent the rest of the afternoon on hold.
Two of the letters were answered; the rest went into a drawer.
Keep what you need and give away the rest.
They met in a bookstore in 1974, and the rest is history.
entries.pronunciation note: the is the weak /ðə/, and it stays /ðə/ in the rest of it because the vowel that follows belongs to the next word — the rest of it /ðə ˈrɛstəvɪt/ · thuh RES-tuh-vit
entries.русский: остальное, остальные — обычное нейтральное слово, о людях, вещах, времени
entries.register: neutral — the ordinary everyday word, at home in every register
entries.type: quantifying pronoun phrase — the noun rest used as a fused head (also a quantifier before of + noun, the rest of the day)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes plural with countables and singular with a mass, a stretch of time, or an abstraction
entries.refers to: everything or everyone left over once part of a set or quantity has been dealt with — people, things, time, money. It takes all of them, which is why it is the default word and the other three in this section are the marked ones.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — The rest of the guests were late (countable → plural); The rest of the milk has gone off (mass → singular); The rest is history (an abstraction, singular). The of-phrase decides, exactly as with all, some, and most.
entries.pattern: the rest [verb] · the rest of [determiner + noun] · the rest of [object pronoun] · [verb] the rest · and the rest, all the rest · for the rest of [time] · the rest is history
entries.contrast: Against the others: the others is countable and plural only and normally means people or discrete things, while the rest takes a mass or a stretch of time just as easily — the rest of the afternoon, the rest of the paint, and ✗the others of the paint is impossible. Against others without the article: that is indefinite, some further ones, where the rest closes the set. Against the remainder and the balance: the same idea in a formal and in a commercial register. The of is obligatory before a pronoun or a determiner — the rest of them, the rest of the cake, ✗the rest them — and bare the rest is used only when the referent is already understood. Keep the pronoun apart from the noun rest meaning repose (a day of rest), which is a different word with a different history.
entries.see also: the remainder, the balance, the majority, others, other, all, some, most, half, the rest of, the remainder of (determiner)

examples: That coffee's gone cold — let me get you another.
He finished the sandwich and immediately ordered another.
Another of the tenants complained about the noise.
One door closed and another opened.
If this pen doesn't work, take another.
She lost one job and found another within the week.

senses.head: One additional item of the same kind
examples: That coffee's gone cold — let me get you another.
He finished the sandwich and immediately ordered another.
Another of the tenants complained about the noise.

senses.head: A different one of the same kind
examples: One door closed and another opened.
If this pen doesn't work, take another.
She lost one job and found another within the week.

entries.pronunciation note: one word, always: ✗an other is not a spelling of it
entries.русский: ещё один; другой — только о счётных, не о массе
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: quantifying and substitute pronoun (also a determiner, another chance)
entries.person / number: third person; singular, always — it contains the article an, so it can be neither plural (✗anothers) nor definite (✗the another)
entries.refers to: one more, or one different, member of a class of countables — things or people. Never a mass: ✗another of the water.
entries.agreement: singular, always — Another is on the way; Another of the pipes has burst.
entries.pattern: another [singular verb] · another of [determiner + plural noun] · another of [object pronoun] · [verb] another (I'll have another) · one … another … · one after another · another two / another three (the one place it precedes a plural, because the numeral makes the phrase a single unit)
entries.contrast: Another vs. other vs. others. Another = one more or one different, singular and indefinite. The other = the remaining one of two. Others = some more, unspecified and plural. The others = all the rest of a definite set. Because another already contains an, the definite and plural jobs have to go to the other forms. Against more: another adds one item, more adds an unmeasured quantity — another coffee is a second cup, more coffee is a refill.
entries.see also: other, others, one, more, each other, another (determiner)

entries.meaning: "And others" — the abbreviation that stands in for every name on a list after the first.
examples: Rivera et al. found no such effect in a sample twice the size.
The case is docketed as Fenwick v. Alameda County et al.
Cite it as (Okonkwo et al., 2019) on first mention and after.
The notice was served on the landlord et al. by certified mail.
Smith et al. have since published a correction.
The grant lists Chen et al. as co-investigators without naming any of them.
entries.pronunciation note: two words, and the period belongs on the second only, because et is a whole Latin word meaning "and" while al. is an abbreviation of alii, aliae, or alia
entries.русский: и др., и другие — книжн., о людях в ссылках и юр. документах; о вещах — etc.
entries.register: formal and scholarly — citations, footnotes, reference lists, case captions, and the address block of a legal notice. An American meets it in a bibliography, on a court docket (Fenwick v. Alameda County et al.), and in the sentence Rivera et al. found no such effect.
entries.type: abbreviated pronominal phrase meaning "and others" — a fused coordinate standing in a noun-phrase slot beside a name
entries.person / number: third person; plural in what it names
entries.refers to: the remaining, unnamed members of a list of people — the co-authors after the first, the additional defendants after the first, the other signatories on a notice. For a list of things the word is etc., and et al. used for things is an error editors correct.
entries.agreement: plural — Rivera et al. find no such effect; Smith et al. have since retracted the paper. The subject means "Rivera and the others," so the verb is plural, and a singular verb (Rivera et al. finds) reads as treating the citation as the name of a paper rather than of its authors. Referring back, the pronoun is they.
entries.pattern: [surname] et al. · [surname] et al. [plural verb] · (Okonkwo et al., 2019) · v. [name] et al. in a case caption · in a reference list, after however many authors the style manual names
entries.variants: the unabbreviated et alii (masculine or mixed), et aliae (feminine), and et alia (neuter), none of which is ever written out in practice; the related scholarly abbreviations et seq. ("and following," for pages and sections), ibid., and id.; the plain-English equivalent and others
entries.contrast: Et al. is for people and etc. is for things — Rivera et al. names co-authors, pencils, erasers, etc. names further items, and swapping the two is the commonest error with either. The period is not optional and belongs where it belongs: et al., never ✗et. al., because et is not an abbreviation, and never ✗et al bare in American style. Against others and the others: the ordinary English pronouns that mean the same thing, and the ones to write in running prose where no citation is being made — Rivera and others have argued is better English in a sentence than Rivera et al. have argued. Whether to italicize is a house matter: Chicago and the APA set it roman, and The Bluebook italicizes it inside a case name.
entries.see also: others, other, the rest, the remainder, such, the aforesaid, the aforementioned, the foregoing, the undersigned, whatnot

examples: I need a screwdriver — do you have one?
The blue one costs twice as much.
She's the one who called the inspector.
Of all the excuses he gave, that was the worst one.
One of the tires was completely flat.
One of my closest friends teaches at the same school.
One does what one can.
One cannot simply walk out of a contract like that.

senses.head: The prop-word
body: Stands in for a countable noun already named, and always carries a determiner or a modifier.
examples: I need a screwdriver — do you have one?
The blue one costs twice as much.
She's the one who called the inspector.
Of all the excuses he gave, that was the worst one.

senses.head: One of + a plural set
examples: One of the tires was completely flat.
One of my closest friends teaches at the same school.

senses.head: The generic or impersonal one
body: Formal; American speech prefers generic you.
examples: One does what one can.
One cannot simply walk out of a contract like that.
