entries.pronunciation note: weak /wən/ when it props up a modifier — the red one /ðə ˈrɛd wən/ · thuh RED wun
entries.русский: слово-заместитель существительного (the red one — красный); тж. обобщённо «человек» — книжн.
entries.case: none for the prop-word; the generic one has the possessive one's and the reflexive oneself
entries.register: the prop-word is neutral; the generic one is formal and noticeably marked in American English
entries.type: prop-word (substitute) pronoun, and separately the generic or impersonal pronoun (also the numeral and the determiner one day)
entries.person / number: third person; singular, with the plural ones
entries.refers to: (1) a countable thing or person already named or understood, so the noun need not be repeated — the red one; (2) people in general including the speaker — one does what one can. Never a mass: there is no ✗a smooth one of the paint.
entries.agreement: singular, always — The blue one is mine; One never knows. The construction to watch is one of + plural noun, which is still singular: One of the windows is broken, never ✗are broken, because the head of the phrase is one.
entries.pattern: [determiner / adjective] one (this one, a big one, the last one) · the one that / who [clause] · which one · one of [determiner + plural noun] + singular verb · generic one [singular verb] … one's … oneself · one another (a separate reciprocal pronoun)
entries.the agreement trap: one of + plural takes a singular verb (One of my friends is a nurse), but a relative clause hanging off the plural noun goes plural, because who points at the noun and not at one — He is one of those people who never apologize. One vs. you: generic one is formal, and American English overwhelmingly prefers generic you (You never know); what is genuinely an error is mixing the two in a single sentence — ✗One should always watch your step. One vs. it: one substitutes for the noun and takes a new referent (I need a pen — do you have one?); it points back at the specific thing already identified (I lost my pen — have you seen it?). And one cannot prop up a mass noun: ✗I'll take the strong one of coffee is not English unless coffee is being counted as cups.
entries.see also: ones, another, each, every one, none, one another, oneself, one (determiner)

examples: The red ones are on sale this week.
Those are the ones we saw at the fair.
I like the ones with the wooden handles.
Which ones did you end up keeping?
The ones who complained loudest never showed up to help.
Take the small ones and leave the rest.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /wənz/ — the red ones /ðə ˈrɛd wənz/
entries.русский: мн. ч. слова-заместителя one — вместо уже названных предметов; без определителя невозможно
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: prop-word (substitute) pronoun — the plural of the prop-word one
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: countable things or people already named, in the plural. It requires a determiner, an adjective, or a relative clause to lean on — bare ones is impossible: ✗I bought ones, ✗Do you have ones?; say some or any instead.
entries.agreement: plural, always — The red ones are cheaper; The ones we saw have already sold.
entries.pattern: [determiner / adjective] ones (the small ones, these ones) · the ones that / who [clause] · which ones · the little ones, the loved ones (semi-lexicalized)
entries.contrast: Ones cannot stand alone, where one can — Do you have one? is fine and ✗Do you have ones? is not; the plural slot is filled by some or any. These ones / those ones are standard in British and Canadian speech but are marked as redundant in American usage, where these and those stand alone: I'll take these, not I'll take these ones. Keep it apart from one's, the possessive of the generic one (one's own business), and from the plural of the numeral (the ones column).
entries.see also: one, others, these, those, one (determiner)

entries.meaning: The second of two, or the one that is left when the first has been accounted for.
examples: One twin went to Boston; the other stayed home.
I have two keys — this one works, and the other doesn't.
She looked at both offers and took the other.
Of the two roads, the other is much faster this time of day.
He kept one copy and mailed the other to his lawyer.
Each brother blamed the other for the mess.
entries.русский: другой — оставшийся член множества, обычно второй из двух
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: substitute pronoun, in practice almost always the other (also a determiner, other people)
entries.person / number: third person; singular in the pronoun form the other; for a plural sense the form must be others or the others
entries.refers to: the remaining member of a set — typically the second of exactly two, when the first has already been named. People or things, countables only.
entries.agreement: singular as the other — The other is broken; The other of the two was never found. If the sense is plural, the word changes shape: the others are.
entries.pattern: the other [singular verb] · one … the other … · [verb] the other · the other of the two · some … other(s) … · each other (a separate reciprocal pronoun)
entries.the set-size rule: with two, one … the other; with more than two, one … another … another …, and the others for all the rest.
entries.contrast: The -s is not optional. Standing alone in a plural sense, the word must be others: ✗Some like it hot; other don't — write others. Standing in front of a noun it must never take the -s: ✗others people. And bare singular other without the is not a modern pronoun: ✗I'll take other — write another or the other.
entries.see also: others, another, one, each other, other (determiner)

entries.meaning: The rest of a group, or some further members of it.
examples: Some of the guests danced; others just watched.
The others had already gone home by the time we arrived.
She finished her section and helped the others with theirs.
A few complained, but others said nothing at all.
Two of the engines were repaired; the others were scrapped.
Others have tried this and failed.
entries.русский: другие; остальные — others «ещё какие-то», the others «все остальные»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: substitute pronoun, plural
entries.person / number: third person; always plural
entries.refers to: additional or remaining people or things. Bare others is indefinite — some more, unspecified; the others is definite — all the rest of a known set.
entries.agreement: plural, always — Others were waiting outside; The others have already left.
entries.pattern: others [plural verb] · the others [plural verb] · some … others … · [verb] the others · others of [noun phrase] (formal) · and others (the English of et al.)
entries.contrast: Others vs. other: the -s appears precisely because no noun follows — other people (determiner, no -s) but others (pronoun, -s required). Others vs. the others: without the, some unspecified additional ones; with the, every remaining member of a definite set — Some left early; others stayed leaves the number open, while Two stayed; the others left closes it. Against another: plural against singular.
entries.see also: other, another, ones, some, each other, other (determiner)

entries.meaning: Points back at a kind of thing just described, or at the situation as a whole.
examples: Such is life.
Such were the terms he insisted on.
He gave no reason, and none was expected; such was his way.
Delays, floods, and the like — such are the risks the policy covers.
Such as remain unsold will be auctioned in the spring.
Such was the state of the roof that two tenants moved out that winter.
She was hired as an interpreter and as such attended every meeting. (fixed adverbial, not the pronoun)
entries.русский: таковой, такие — книжн. и юр., о только что описанном, часто о целой ситуации
entries.register: formal, legal, and literary — the pronoun use is not ordinary conversational English
entries.type: substitute pronoun (also a determiner, such nonsense, and a predeterminer, such a mess)
entries.person / number: third person; invariant; construes singular or plural with the referent
entries.refers to: things or people of the kind just described, or a whole preceding situation taken as a lump (Such was the state of the roof). Its antecedent is often an entire clause rather than a noun phrase.
entries.agreement: agrees with what it refers to — Such are the risks (plural referent); Such is life (singular). The verb typically inverts with it, since the pronoun is fronted.
entries.pattern: such [verb] [subject complement] (Such is the case) · such as [clause] (formal: such as remain) · as such (fixed adverbial) · and such (informal: tools and such) · no such thing (determiner) · legal such + noun (such defects, a determiner)
entries.contrast: As a bare pronoun such has narrowed to a handful of frames — such is life, such was the case, such are the risks, such as remain. Everywhere else American English fills the slot with that, this, or those: Such was his answer → That was his answer. The legal such of such agreement and such party is a determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary. And as such traditionally means "in that capacity" or "strictly speaking," and it wants a noun antecedent to point back at: He is the treasurer and as such signs the checks. The causal as such meaning "therefore" — It rained; as such, we stayed in — has spread widely through business and academic prose, but there is no antecedent there for such to refer to, and the usage is still objected to often enough that therefore, so, or for that reason is the safer word.
entries.see also: so, that, those, others, such (determiner)

entries.meaning: The particular member that the words around it identify — the definite half of the prop-word one.
examples: The one on the left has a chip in it.
She's the one who called the inspector.
Of the four keys he tried, the one that worked was the oldest.
That's the one — the blue folder on top of the pile.
He's convinced she's the one, and they have known each other three weeks.
Tell them the one about the mule.
The ones we saw at the fair were half the price. (plural)
entries.pronunciation note: one begins with the consonant /w/, so the takes its ordinary weak form /ðə/ and not the pre-vowel /ði/; the /ði/ form appears only under contrastive stress, which is exactly what he's THE one is doing
entries.русский: тот самый — тот член множества, который выделяет следующее уточнение
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: definite prop-word (substitute) pronoun phrase — the prop-word one with the definite article, used as a fused head
entries.person / number: third person; singular, with the plural the ones
entries.refers to: the particular member of a set that a following modifier, a relative clause, or the situation identifies — a thing or a person. It needs that identification: bare the one with nothing to pin it down works only where the context has already done the pinning (That's the one).
entries.agreement: singular — The one on the left is cracked; The one who called was her brother. The plural the ones takes a plural verb: The ones we saw have already sold. As a subject complement it does not control the verb at all — You are the one who decides — and the relative clause inside one of those people who… goes plural, a trap dealt with at one.
entries.pattern: the one + prepositional phrase (the one on the left) · the one + relative clause (the one that broke, the one who called) · the one with / in / about · that's the one, he's the one, she's not the one · the one about + a joke · plural the ones
entries.variants: the plural the ones, which behaves the same way and is dictionaried at ones; the demonstrative alternatives this one and that one
entries.contrast: Against bare prop-word one: one is indefinite and introduces a fresh instance (I need a pen — do you have one?), while the one is definite and picks a known instance out of a set (the one in the drawer). Against ones: a difference of number only, with the caution that bare ones cannot stand alone where one can. Against this one and that one: the demonstratives point, while the one identifies by description, which is why something almost always follows it. Two idioms are worth naming, and both live entirely off the definite article — the one meaning the destined person (He thinks she's the one) and the one introducing a joke (the one about the mule).
entries.see also: one, ones, another, other, the usual, this one / that one, those who, he who, he that, she who, they that, one (determiner)

entries.ipa: /ðə ˈjuʒuəl/, in ordinary speech /ðə ˈjuʒwəl/ and /ðə ˈjuʒəl/
entries.meaning: Whatever both of you already know is habitual — the fused head that runs entirely on shared knowledge.
examples: The usual, please, and put it on my tab.
He asked how the week had gone and she said, the usual.
The usual was waiting for him at the end of the bar before he sat down.
They wanted an explanation and got the usual.
Breakfast was the usual — eggs, toast, and the crossword.
The usual has been happening at that intersection since they changed the light.
entries.pronunciation note: three syllables said carefully and two said quickly; the is the weak /ðə/ before the consonantal /j/
entries.русский: как обычно, обычное — разг., то, что собеседник и так знает по привычке
entries.register: informal to neutral — the language of bars, diners, and standing arrangements, and of dry understatement in writing
entries.type: fused-head pronoun phrase — the adjective usual standing where its noun would be (also the ordinary adjective, the usual suspects)
entries.person / number: third person; singular
entries.refers to: whatever the hearer already knows to be habitual — the drink you always order, the excuse he always gives, the trouble that always happens there. Its antecedent is shared knowledge rather than anything on the page, which is why the phrase works across a bar and fails in a document.
entries.agreement: singular — The usual is waiting for you at the end of the bar; The usual has been happening at that intersection all year. Where the referent is plainly plural the fused head turns unnatural and the noun comes back: the usual complaints were filed, not ✗the usual were filed.
entries.pattern: [verb] the usual (I'll have the usual) · the usual [singular verb] · the usual from [somewhere] · as a bare answer (How was your week? — The usual.) · as usual, business as usual (fixed adverbials, not this pronoun) · the usual suspects, the usual channels (the adjective in front of a noun)
entries.contrast: Against the same: the same points back at something just named (I'll have the same), while the usual points at a standing habit that may never have been mentioned — the two are close, and the difference is where the antecedent lives. Against such and the like: those generalize about a kind of thing, this identifies one habitual instance. Against as usual: a fixed adverbial and a different word class, since as usual, he was late modifies the clause while I'll have the usual fills an object slot. Because the phrase runs on shared knowledge, never in writing for a reader who does not already have it: in a report, name the thing.
entries.see also: the one, such, the same, the like, so, whatnot, the occasional (determiner)

entries.meaning: A bare number standing where its noun would be — the plainest fused head in the language. --- ← The grammar of pronouns · All categories
examples: We ordered six chairs and two arrived broken.
Three of them had never been opened.
She read the first chapter twice and skipped the next two.
Of the twelve applications, only four were complete.
I'll take a dozen, and make half of them plain.
Two of us stayed behind to lock up.
He asked for volunteers and a dozen put their hands up.
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of to and too, and unlike them it never reduces — the numeral keeps its full vowel and normally carries stress, which is the audible difference between I have two and I have to
entries.русский: двое, две штуки — числительное-заместитель уже названных счётных предметов
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: cardinal numeral used as a fused head — the numeral standing where its noun would be (also a determiner, two chairs, and an ordinary noun, the number two)
entries.person / number: third person; plural for every cardinal from two upward; one is the singular member of the series and is dictionaried at one
entries.refers to: the stated number of countable things or people already named or understood. Never a mass: ✗two of the water. The numeral counts exactly, which is the one thing that separates it from every other pronoun in this dictionary.
entries.agreement: plural, always, from two up — Two were missing; Two of the panels have come loose; A dozen were broken in shipping. Note that a dozen is plural in the same way in spite of its singular article, because the head of the phrase is a number and not a noun.
entries.pattern: [numeral] [plural verb] (Three arrived) · [numeral] of [determiner + plural noun] · [numeral] of [object pronoun] · [verb] [numeral] (I'll take three) · the first two, all three, any two, another two · a dozen, half a dozen, a hundred, a thousand on the same pattern
entries.variants: every cardinal above one — three, four, ten, forty-one — and the countable group nouns used the same way: a dozen, half a dozen, a pair, a score, a hundred, a thousand. The indefinite plurals dozens, hundreds, and thousands are a different construction and are at hundreds.
entries.contrast: The numeral is a pronoun only when the noun is gone. Two chairs are missing is a determiner in front of a noun and belongs to the determiner dictionary; Two are missing is this pronoun. Against a couple: two is exact and a couple approximate in ordinary American use, which is why an invoice says two and a story says a couple. Against both: both also names two, but it insists that they are the two already known and that neither is left out — Two of them agreed comes out of an open set, Both of them agreed out of a set of exactly two. Against hundreds and dozens: the -s turns an exact count into an estimate. And the of is obligatory before a determiner or a pronoun: two of the panels, two of them, ✗two them.
entries.see also: one, ones, both, a couple, a few, hundreds, a third, one or more, two, three, four (determiner), dozen (determiner), one (determiner)
